Scalable Utility-Aware Multiclass Calibration

 

Mahmoud Hegazy          Michael I. Jordan          Aymeric Dieuleveut

CMAP, École polytechnique, IP Paris, France; Inria Paris, France          Inria Paris, France; EECS, UC Berkeley, USA          CMAP, École polytechnique, IP Paris, France

Abstract

Ensuring that classifiers are well-calibrated, i.e., their predictions align with observed frequencies, is a minimal and fundamental requirement for classifiers to be viewed as trustworthy. Existing methods for assessing multiclass calibration often focus on specific aspects associated with prediction (e.g., top-class confidence, class-wise calibration) or utilize computationally challenging variational formulations. In this work, we study scalable evaluation of multiclass calibration. To this end, we propose utility calibration, a general framework that measures the calibration error relative to a specific utility function that encapsulates the goals or decision criteria relevant to the end user. We demonstrate how this framework can unify and re-interpret several existing calibration metrics, particularly allowing for more robust versions of the top-class and class-wise calibration metrics, and, going beyond such binarized approaches, toward assessing calibration for richer classes of downstream utilities.

1 INTRODUCTION

Calibration is a fundamental property of probabilistic predictors. A calibrated model produces predictions that, on average, align with observed frequencies. For instance, if a weather forecaster predicts a 30% chance of rain on a given day, rain should occur on approximately 30% of such days. In multiclass classification problems, calibration ensures that the predicted probabilities reflect the true likelihood of each class. Formally, let 𝒳\mathcal{X} denote the input space, 𝒴={e1,…,eC}\mathcal{Y}=\{e_{1},\ldots,e_{C}\} the output space, where eie_{i} is the ii-th canonical basis vector in ℝC\mathbb{R}^{C}, and ΔC−1≔{x∈ℝ+C|∑ixi=1}\Delta^{C-1}\coloneqq\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{C}|\sum_{i}x_{i}=1\right\} denote the simplex in ℝC\mathbb{R}^{C}. A predictor f:𝒳→ΔC−1f:\mathcal{X}\to\Delta^{C-1} is said to be perfectly calibrated with respect to a distribution DD over 𝒳×𝒴\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y} if 𝔼⁡[Y∣f⁡(X)]=f⁡(X)\mathbb{E}[Y\mid f(X)]=f(X). The most direct metric for quantifying the deviation from perfect calibration is the Mean Calibration Error (MCE\mathrm{MCE}).

Definition 1.1 (Mean Calibration Error).

For a distribution DD such that (X,Y)∼D(X,Y)\sim D and a predictor ff, the mean calibration error is defined as MCE⁡(f)≔𝔼[‖𝔼⁡[Y∣f⁡(X)]−f⁡(X)‖2].\mathrm{MCE}(f)\coloneqq\expec\left[\left\lVert\mathbb{E}[Y\mid f(X)]-f(X)\right\rVert_{2}\right].

Without further assumptions, the MCE\mathrm{MCE} is fundamentally impossible to estimate, even in the binary setting (Lee et al., 2023; Duchi, 2024). While assumptions like Hölder continuity of 𝔼[Y|f⁡(X)]\expec\left[Y|f(X)\right] allow for consistent estimators of 𝔼[Y|f⁡(X)]\expec\left[Y|f(X)\right] or minimax optimal tests for MCE⁡(f)\mathrm{MCE}(f) (Lee et al., 2023; Popordanoska et al., 2022; Tsybakov, 2009), their sample complexity scales exponentially with the dimension CC.

Due to the difficulty of measuring MCE\mathrm{MCE}, multiple relaxations have been proposed, falling into two main categories: binarized and variational. First, binarized approaches (Gupta and Ramdas, 2022; Panchenko et al., 2022; Guo et al., 2017) simplify the problem by focusing on specific binary events derived from the multiclass predictions, e.g. top-class or class-wise calibration. However, these methods are by nature presumptive of downstream tasks. Moreover, their reliance on binning schemes or kernel estimators for the underlying binary subproblems introduces sensitivity to estimator choices and can suffer from high bias (Roelofs et al., 2022). Second, variational approaches (Jung et al., 2021; Błasiok et al., 2023; Gopalan et al., 2024; Kumar et al., 2018; Widmann et al., 2019; Zhao et al., 2021) assess calibration through optimization problems, such as the distance to the nearest perfectly calibrated predictor or the worst-case error against a class of witness functions. Unfortunately, these methods can be computationally intensive and can scale poorly in CC.

To address these limitations and provide an application-focused perspective on calibration, we introduce utility calibration. This framework evaluates a model ff by considering a downstream user who employs its predictions f⁡(X)f(X). The core idea is to measure calibration error relative to a specific utility function, denoted uu, which encapsulates the goals, costs, or decision criteria relevant to this end user. Utility calibration then assesses how well the expected utility (as estimated by the user based on f⁡(X)f(X) and uu) aligns with the realized utility (obtained when the true outcome YY is observed).

In practice, models often serve diverse users or a single user with multiple objectives. We thus extend utility calibration to handle classes of utility functions. The overall utility calibration for a class 𝒰\cal U can be defined as the worst-case error over u∈𝒰u\in{\cal U}, denoted UC⁡(f,𝒰)\mathrm{UC}(f,{\cal U}). A notable aspect of this formulation is that it provides a structured way to express and analyze various existing calibration notions. In particular, by defining appropriate utility functions within 𝒰{\cal U}, concepts such as top-class and class-wise calibration can be cast within the utility calibration framework. This offers a unified perspective and a superior alternative to binning for examining those notions of calibration.

Contributions and outline:

In Section 2, we review related literature on calibration metrics and post-hoc calibration methods. In Section 3, we define utility calibration and relate it to existing measures of calibration. In addition, we demonstrate how this framework can be used to frame several existing calibration concepts within a common utility-aware perspective, offering consistent interpretations and providing examples of relevant utility classes. Then, in Section 4, to characterize the difficulty of achieving utility calibration for classes of utility functions, we introduce the notions of proactive and interactive measurability. While for rich utility classes, proactive measurability is not possible, we show that interactive measurability is achievable for many classes of interest. Drawing on these insights, in Section 5, we empirically demonstrate the application of our proposed metrics and evaluation methodology. While the main motivation of this work is developing a better methodology for calibration assessment, we also show that our framework naturally yields a simple patching-style post-hoc calibration algorithm that achieves competitive performance against commonly used post-hoc calibration methods.

2 RELATED WORK

In this section, we review three classical and related approaches to measuring or ensuring a form of calibration, namely post-hoc calibration methods, binarized relaxations, and variational approaches.

First, post-hoc calibration refers to techniques applied to a pre-trained model’s outputs to improve the alignment between its predicted probabilities and the true likelihood of outcomes without altering the original model parameters. Such methods are advantageous as they decouple calibration concerns from model training.

Popular post-hoc calibration algorithms include Temperature Scaling and its multi-parameter extensions, Vector Scaling and Matrix Scaling (Guo et al., 2017), which may all be regarded as a multiclass extension of Platt’s scaling (Platt et al., 1999). Dirichlet calibration assumes the model’s predicted probability vectors can be modeled by a Dirichlet distribution, whose parameters are learned on a calibration set to transform the original probabilities (Kull et al., 2019). Nonparametric methods such as Histogram Binning (Zadrozny and Elkan, 2001) and Isotonic Regression (Zadrozny and Elkan, 2002) learn calibration maps by discretizing the probability space or fitting monotonic (order-preserving) functions, respectively. Other methods also include: (Patel et al., 2020), which applies a specific binning strategy followed by recalibration to minimize class-wise calibration error, (Rahimi et al., 2020), which uses order-preserving transformations for recalibration to maintain accuracy. Finally, a related body of literature aims to improve calibration by regularizing the training objective, e.g. (Mukhoti et al., 2020; Popordanoska et al., 2022; Marx et al., 2024).

While post-hoc methods aim to minimize the calibration error, assessing the calibration error itself remains a non-trivial task. Binarized relaxations aim to circumvent the difficulty of measuring the calibration error of a high-dimensional predictor ff by measuring the MCE\mathrm{MCE} of a single or multiple downstream binary versions of ff instead. Two commonly used relaxations are the Top-Class calibration Error (TCE\mathrm{TCE}) (Guo et al., 2017) and the Class-Wise calibration Error (CWE\mathrm{CWE}) (Panchenko et al., 2022), defined as

TCE⁡(f)\displaystyle\mathrm{TCE}(f) =𝔼[|𝔼[Y∗∣p∗]−p∗|],\displaystyle=\expec\big[\,|\,\expec[Y_{*}\mid p_{*}]-p_{*}\,|\,\big],
CWE⁡(f)\displaystyle\mathrm{CWE}(f) =∑i∈[C]wi𝔼[|𝔼[𝟙Y=ei∣fi]−fi|],\displaystyle=\sum_{i\in[C]}w_{i}\,\expec\big[\,|\,\expec[\mathbbm{1}_{Y=e_{i}}\mid f_{i}]-f_{i}\,|\,\big],

with the shorthands fi≔f​(X)if_{i}\coloneqq f(X)_{i}, p∗≔f​(X)i∗p_{*}\coloneq f(X)_{i_{*}}, and Y∗≔𝟙Y=ei∗Y_{*}\coloneq\mathbbm{1}_{Y=e_{i_{*}}}, where i∗≔argmaxi​f​(X)ii_{*}\coloneq\mathrm{argmax}_{i}f(X)_{i}. In addition, wiw_{i} is a class-dependent weight, which can be set to 1/C1/C, wi=ℙ{Y=ei}w_{i}=\prob\{Y=e_{i}\}, or another choice w∈ΔC−1w\in\Delta^{C-1}.

Both TCE\mathrm{TCE} and CWE\mathrm{CWE} require the estimation of conditional expectation, which is typically approximated using binning schemes. For (Bj)j∈[m](B_{j})_{j\in[m]} a partition of [0,1][0,1], the binned estimators are

TCEbin​(f)=∑j∈[m]|𝔼[(p∗−Y∗)​𝟙p∗∈Bj]|\mathrm{TCE}^{\mathrm{bin}}(f)=\sum_{j\in[m]}\big|\expec\left[(p_{*}-Y_{*})\mathbbm{1}_{p_{*}\in B_{j}}\right]\big| (2.1)
CWEbin​(f)=∑i∈[C],j∈[m]wi​|𝔼[(fi−𝟙Y=ei)​𝟙fi∈Bj]|.\mathrm{CWE}^{\mathrm{bin}}(f)=\sum_{\mathclap{{i\in[C],j\in[m]}}}w_{i}\left\lvert\expec\left[\big(f_{i}-\mathbbm{1}_{Y=e_{i}}\big)\mathbbm{1}_{f_{i}\in B_{j}}\right]\right\rvert. (2.2)

Gupta and Ramdas (2022) unified multiple instances of binarized proxies of MCE\mathrm{MCE}, such as TCE,CWE\mathrm{TCE},\mathrm{CWE} and topK\mathrm{topK} confidence calibration, introduced in (Gupta et al., 2021), and proposed additional binarized reductions which offer stronger notions of calibration. Unfortunately, the binning schemes used in such binarized proxies are known to have a large effect on the estimated error (Roelofs et al., 2022; Gruber and Buettner, 2022). Apart from the simpler equal-size bins (Guo et al., 2017) and equal-weight bins (Zadrozny and Elkan, 2001), multiple binning schemes built on top of different heuristics have been proposed (Roelofs et al., 2022; Patel et al., 2020; Naeini et al., 2015; Nixon et al., , see, e.g.,). Gupta and Ramdas (2021) showed a simple equal-weight binning scheme with better sample complexity guarantees for estimating bin averages. Kumar et al. (2019) developed adaptive binning schemes with guarantees for discrete ff and showed that for any binning scheme, there exists a worst-case continuous ff such that the bias of TCEbin​(f)\mathrm{TCE}^{\mathrm{bin}}(f) as an estimate of TCE⁡(f)\mathrm{TCE}(f) is lower bounded by 0.490.49 (noting that TCE\mathrm{TCE} is bounded between 00 and 11).

On the other hand, there exist binning-free alternatives for binarized reductions (Popordanoska et al., 2022; Gupta et al., 2021, see, e.g.,). Nonetheless, in an assumption-free setting, it is generally impossible to consistently estimate the MCE\mathrm{MCE} of binary predictors (Lee et al., 2023; Duchi, 2024; Rossellini et al., 2025). As such, it is generally difficult to control the calibration error defined by binarized relaxations.

On the other hand, variational approaches do not strictly aim to measure the MCE\mathrm{MCE}. Instead, they consider alternative formulations that do not require direct estimation of the conditional expectation. For example, Distance to Calibration (DC\mathrm{DC}) measures the distance between ff and the nearest perfectly calibrated predictors (Błasiok et al., 2023):

DC⁡(f)≔infMCE⁡(g)=0𝔼⁡[‖f⁡(X)−g⁡(X)‖1].\mathrm{DC}(f)\,\coloneqq\,\inf_{\mathrm{MCE}(g)=0}\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[\|f(X)-g(X)\|_{1}\bigr].

A unified formulation of variational measures of calibration is weighted calibration, which assesses the calibration error against a class of witness functions (Jung et al., 2021). Concretely, let 𝒲\mathcal{W} be a class of functions mapping ΔC−1\Delta^{C-1} to [−1,1]C[-1,1]^{C}. Then, weighted calibration error with witness class 𝒲\mathcal{W} is

CE𝒲​(f)=supw∈𝒲𝔼X,Y​[⟨w⁡(f⁡(X)),f⁡(X)−Y⟩].\mathrm{CE}_{\mathcal{W}}(f)=\mathop{\sup}_{w\in\mathcal{W}}\mathbb{E}_{X,Y}\left[\left\langle w\bigl(f(X)\bigr),f(X)-Y\right\rangle\right]. (2.3)

A specific instance of weighted calibration is the Kernel Calibration Error (KCE) (Lin et al., 2023), which sets 𝒲\mathcal{W} to be the unit ball of the reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) of a multivariate universal kernel. This allows for efficient computation of the supremum but it remains hard to interpret the impact of low KCE for a user of ff. Błasiok et al. (2023) showed that in the binary setting, DC⁡(f)\mathrm{DC}(f) and CELip⁡(1)​(f)\mathrm{CE}_{\mathrm{Lip(1)}}(f) are equivalent up to a (low-degree) polynomial scaling and that CELip⁡(1)​(f)\mathrm{CE}_{\mathrm{Lip}(1)}(f) can be well approximated by the RKHS of the Laplace kernel, where Lip⁡(1)\mathrm{Lip}(1) is the class of 11-Lipschitz functions from ΔC−1\Delta^{C-1} to [−1,1][-1,1].

The result on the equivalence between CELip⁡(1)​(f)\mathrm{CE}_{\mathrm{Lip}(1)}(f) and DC⁡(f)\mathrm{DC}(f) was further extended to the multiclass setting in (Duchi, 2024, Theorem 15.5.5) and (Gopalan et al., 2024, Lemma 3.3). In particular, Gopalan et al. (2022a) showed that measuring either DC⁡(f)\mathrm{DC}(f) or CELip⁡(1)​(f)\mathrm{CE}_{\mathrm{Lip}(1)}(f) requires an exponential number of samples in CC (Gopalan et al., 2024, Theorem 3.2. and Theorem 3.4.). Thus, even though DC⁡(f)\mathrm{DC}\left(f\right) can be efficiently assessed in the binary setting, it is quickly intractable as CC increases.

A particular case is Decision calibration, introduced by Zhao et al. (2021), that tailors calibration guarantees to downstream decision-making tasks. A predictor ff is considered decision calibrated of order KK if, for any decision problem involving at most KK actions, the expected loss computed using the model’s predictions f⁡(X)f(X) accurately matches the true expected loss incurred. Formally, for any loss function ℓ\ell mapping an outcome-action pair to a real-valued loss, decision calibration of order KK requires:

𝔼⁡[ℓ⁡(Y^,δ⁡(f⁡(X)))]=𝔼⁡[ℓ⁡(Y,δ⁡(f⁡(X)))].\mathbb{E}\big[\ell\big(\hat{Y},\delta(f(X))\big)\big]\,=\,\mathbb{E}\big[\ell\big(Y,\delta(f(X))\big)\big].

where Y^∼f⁡(X)\hat{Y}\sim f(X) and δ\delta is a decision rule that picks the best action among KK actions under the model’s prediction f⁡(X)f(X). This ensures that decision-makers can reliably estimate the consequences of actions when using the predictor. A key contribution of Zhao et al. (2021) is showing that decision calibration of order KK can be achieved by having supp∈P⁡(K)∥𝔼[(Y−f(X))𝟙{f(X)∈p}]∥=0\sup_{p\in P(K)}\|\expec[(Y-f(X))\mathbbm{1}\left\{f(X)\in p\right\}]\|=0, where P⁡(K)P(K) is the set of polytopes with at most KK supporting hyperplanes. Moreover, low decision calibration guarantees a notion of no-regret to downstream users, i.e., they cannot improve their utility by using any other best response policy; associated with another loss ℓ′\ell^{\prime} instead of ℓ\ell.

In a similar aim to Zhao et al. (2021), multiple works have studied calibration through a downstream decision-theoretic perspective. Broadly, two complementary approaches have emerged: (i) online, regret-driven forecasting that enforces event-conditional notions of calibration and yields no (swap)-regret guarantees for best-responding agents (Noarov et al., 2025; Roth and Shi, 2024); and (ii) decision-centric objectives that guarantee good performance across rich families of utilities or proper scoring rules, e.g., U-calibration (Kleinberg et al., 2023).

Foundationally, these formulations target an ambitious goal, ensuring that downstream agents who best-respond using the predictor ff achieve (near-)optimal utility across scenarios and losses. However, this ambition often comes with scalability costs: U-calibration is developed in the binary online setting; the swap-regret guarantees in Roth and Shi (2024) rely on Lipschitz utilities in low dimensions (e.g., d∈{1,2}d\in\{1,2\}) and, in higher dimensions, assume a bounded action set and smooth best responses; and measuring decision calibration is computationally intractable in CC, with exponential complexity even for K=2K=2 (Gopalan et al., 2024).

By contrast, we adopt a scalable assessment perspective. Our utility calibration (shortly introduced in Section 3) requires that the predicted utility vu​(X)v_{u}(X) is a reliable regressor of the realized utility u⁡(f⁡(X),Y)u(f(X),Y). This prioritizes the reliability of utility estimation–not enforcing optimal downstream decisions–so users can recognize when their expected utility is poor rather than be misled by optimistic forecasts. Operationally, it reduces multiclass assessment to a binning-free worst-interval deviation in vuv_{u}, scales well with CC, and supports interactively measurable audits across broad utility classes, complementing online/regret-focused formulations.

3 UTILITY CALIBRATION (UC)

We consider the following utility-centric formulation of calibration. In particular, we are interested in the setting where, for some input XX, a downstream user leverages f⁡(X)f(X) as an estimate of 𝔼[Y∣X]\expec\left[Y\mid X\right]. Based on this estimate of the conditional expectation, the user may then take arbitrary actions or decisions. Finally, the user observes the true realization of the label YY and, based on this realization, may then suffer some loss or achieve some gain. To model such a pipeline of observation, action, then consequences, we consider a utility function u:ΔC−1×𝒴→[−1,1]u:\Delta^{C-1}\times\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow[-1,1] such that u⁡(f⁡(X),Y)u(f(X),Y) models the reward obtained or the loss suffered by the decision-makers after using f⁡(X)f(X) to take arbitrary actions/decisions. In such a setting, predictability is highly desirable, in the sense that when using the predictor ff, the utility obtained is similar to the utility expected. More concretely, for Y^∼f⁡(X)\hat{Y}\sim f(X) and a given input XX, the user can use f⁡(X)f(X) to construct the following estimate of utility:

vu​(X)≔𝔼[u⁡(f⁡(X),Y^)∣X]=⟨f⁡(X),u→​(X)⟩,v_{u}(X)\coloneqq\expec\left[u(f(X),\hat{Y})\mid X\right]=\left\langle f(X),\vec{u}(X)\right\rangle, (3.1)

where u→:𝒳→[−1,1]C\vec{u}:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow[-1,1]^{C} is defined as u→​(X)≔(u⁡(f⁡(X),ei))i∈[C]\vec{u}(X)\coloneqq(u\left(f(X),e_{i}\right))_{i\in[C]}. Ideally, we want the function vu​(X)v_{u}(X) to be an unbiased estimator of the true utility. As such, we define the utility calibration with respect to a utility function uu, denoted by UC⁡(f,u)\mathrm{UC}\left(f,u\right), as

supI∈𝕀⁡[−1,1]|𝔼[(u⁡(f⁡(X),Y)−vu​(X))​𝟙vu​(X)∈I]|.\sup_{I\in\mathbb{I}\left[-1,1\right]}\left\lvert\expec\left[(u(f(X),Y)-v_{u}(X))\mathbbm{1}_{v_{u}(X)\in I}\right]\right\rvert. (3.2)

We say that ff is ε\varepsilon-calibrated with respect to a utility function uu if UC⁡(f,u)≤ε\mathrm{UC}(f,u)\leq\varepsilon. Note that for I=[a,b]I=[a,b], the inner term in (3.2) can be rewritten as

|𝔼[(u⁡(f⁡(X),Y)−vu​(X))|vu​(X)∈[a,b]]|​pa,b,\left\lvert\expec\left[\left(u(f(X),Y)-v_{u}(X)\right)\big|v_{u}(X)\in[a,b]\right]\right\rvert p_{a,b},

where pa,b=ℙ{vu(X)∈[a,b]}p_{a,b}=\prob\left\{v_{u}(X)\in[a,b]\right\}. In words, looking at the instances where vu​(X)∈[a,b]v_{u}(X)\in[a,b], the bias between the utility the decision-maker expects to get (while using f⁡(X)f(X) to take decisions and to estimate the utility) and the actual utility the decision-maker achieves (when using f⁡(X)f(X) to take decisions), is at most ε\varepsilon after being weighted by the probability of {vu(X)∈[a,b]}\left\{v_{u}(X)\in[a,b]\right\}.

Combining (3.1) and (3.2) above, one obtains that UC⁡(f,u)\mathrm{UC}\left(f,u\right) is equivalent to

supI∈𝕀⁡[−1,1]|𝔼[⟨Y−f(X),u→(X)⟩𝟙{vu(X)∈I}]|.\sup_{I\in\mathbb{I}\left[-1,1\right]}\left|\expec\!\left[\left\langle Y-f(X),\vec{u}(X)\right\rangle\mathbbm{1}\{v_{u}(X)\in I\}\right]\right|. (3.3)

Thus, utility calibration is equivalent to weighted calibration (2.3), with the witness class 𝒲\mathcal{W} set to 𝒲(u)≔{x↦ξu→(x)𝟙{vu(x)∈I}|I∈𝕀[−1,1]}\mathcal{W}\left(u\right)\coloneqq\left\{x\mapsto\xi\vec{u}(x)\mathbbm{1}\left\{v_{u}(x)\in I\right\}|I\in\mathbb{I}\left[-1,1\right]\right\}. In addition, our notion of utility calibration requires that the predicted label Y^∼f⁡(X)\hat{Y}\sim f(X) can be used for an unbiased estimate of the utility. This is related to Outcome Indistinguishability (OI) (Dwork et al., 2021), where a predictor ff is considered reliable if its simulated outcomes Y^∼f⁡(X)\hat{Y}\sim f(X) are computationally indistinguishable from Nature’s true outcomes YY. We also note that this perspective connects to recent work that leverages OI variants to establish links between loss minimization guarantees, omnipredictors, and multicalibration (Gopalan et al., 2022b; Gopalan et al., 2023a; Gopalan et al., 2023b).

3.1 Decision-Theoretic Implications of UC

In a recent work, for the binary classification setting, Rossellini et al. (2025) introduced the CutOff calibration metric, which assesses the calibration error by measuring against the worst-case bin, and demonstrated that it provides robust decision-theoretic guarantees. We defer a more detailed discussion of CutOff calibration to Appendix B.1. By assessing the UC⁡(f,u)\mathrm{UC}\left(f,u\right) on the worst-case interval of vu​(⋅)v_{u}(\cdot), our construction of utility calibration can be seen as a generalization of CutOff calibration to multiple dimensions and arbitrary utility functions, and it in fact inherits analogous decision-theoretic guarantees to those shown in Rossellini et al. (2025, Prop 2.1 and 3.2).

In particular, consider a decision rule based on thresholding the predicted utility vu​(X)v_{u}(X) at some level t0∈[−1,1]t_{0}\in[-1,1], i.e., taking the action U^t0≔𝟙{vu(X)≥t0}\hat{U}_{t_{0}}\coloneqq\mathbbm{1}\left\{v_{u}(X)\geq t_{0}\right\}. This models the situation in which a user needs to commit a binary decision after estimating the utility using f⁡(X)f(X). Then, the quality of this decision can be assessed by the loss ℓutil(u~,U^;t)=|u~−t|𝟙{U^≠𝟙{u≥t}}\ell_{\mathrm{util}}(\tilde{u},\widehat{U};t)=\left\lvert\tilde{u}-t\right\rvert\mathbbm{1}\{\hat{U}\neq\mathbbm{1}\left\{u\geq t\right\}\}, which penalizes the deviation between the true utility uYu_{Y} and the decision threshold t0t_{0} when a mismatch between U^t0\hat{U}_{t_{0}} and the ideal decision occurs. Consequently, let Rutil​(g,t0)=𝔼⁡[ℓutil​(u⁡(f⁡(X),Y),U^t0,t0)]R_{\mathrm{util}}(g;t_{0})=\mathbb{E}[\ell_{\mathrm{util}}(u(f(X),Y),\hat{U}_{t_{0}};t_{0})] be the associated risk. Then, we show that the decision process U^t0\hat{U}_{t_{0}} cannot significantly be improved by any simple post-processing of vu​(⋅)v_{u}(\cdot) through a composition with a monotone function.

Proposition 3.1 (Utility Risk Gap).

For any utility uu and threshold t0∈[−1,1]t_{0}\in[-1,1],

Rutil​(vuCLOSE\displaystyle R_{\mathrm{util}}(v_{u} OPEN(X);t0)−\displaystyle(X);t_{0})-
infh:[−1,1]→[−1,1]monotoneRutil(h(vu(X));t0)≤2UC(f,u).\displaystyle\inf_{\begin{subarray}{c}h:[-1,1]\to[-1,1]\\ \textnormal{monotone}\end{subarray}}R_{\mathrm{util}}(h(v_{u}(X));t_{0})\leq 2\,\mathrm{UC}(f,u).

In words, Proposition 3.1 indicates that, if ff is utility calibrated, in such a binary decision-making scenario, the user can barely benefit from any monotonic post-processing to vuv_{u}. Another interpretation of vu​(X)v_{u}(X) is as a regressor for the realized utility uY≔u⁡(f⁡(X),Y)∈[−1,1]u_{Y}\coloneqq u(f(X),Y)\in[-1,1]. Similar to Rossellini et al. (2025, Prop 2.1), we can show that the regressor vuv_{u} satisfies a notion of calibration itself. First, note that distance from calibration naturally extends to such a single-dimension regression problem by considering a function gu​(X)g_{u}(X) to be a perfectly calibrated predictor of uYu_{Y} if 𝔼⁡[uY∣gu​(X)]=gu​(X)\mathbb{E}[u_{Y}\mid g_{u}(X)]=g_{u}(X), a.s. We denote this extended notion of distance from calibration as DCU⁡(f,u)\mathrm{DCU}(f,u), the Distance to Calibrated Utility Predictor for vu​(X)v_{u}(X) with respect to the realized utility u⁡(f⁡(X),Y)u(f(X),Y):

DCU⁡(f)\displaystyle\mathrm{DCU}\left(f\right) ≔infgu:𝒳→[−1,1]𝔼|gu(X)−vu(X)|\displaystyle\coloneqq\inf_{g_{u}:\mathcal{X}\to[-1,1]}\;\mathbb{E}\left|g_{u}(X)-v_{u}(X)\right|
s.t. ​𝔼​[uY∣gu​(X)]=gu​(X).\displaystyle\text{s.t. }\;\mathbb{E}[u_{Y}\mid g_{u}(X)]=g_{u}(X)\,.

We show that DCU⁡(f,u)\mathrm{DCU}(f,u) can be effectively controlled through UC⁡(f,u)\mathrm{UC}(f,u).

Proposition 3.2 (Utility Calibration Upper Bounds DCU\mathrm{DCU}).

Let u:ΔC−1×𝒴→[−1,1]u:\Delta^{C-1}\times\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow[-1,1] be a utility function. Then,

DCU⁡(f)≤8​UC​(f,u)+UC⁡(f,u).\mathrm{DCU}\left(f\right)\;\leq\;\sqrt{8\,\mathrm{UC}(f,u)}+\mathrm{UC}(f,u).

Proposition 3.2 implies that if UC⁡(f,u)\mathrm{UC}(f,u) is small, then vu​(X)v_{u}(X), seen as a regressor for the true utility u⁡(f⁡(X),Y)u(f(X),Y), is a calibrated predictor itself. This further strengthens the interpretation of UC⁡(f,u)\mathrm{UC}(f,u): not only does it ensure actionable decisions based on vu​(X)v_{u}(X), but it also guarantees that vu​(X)v_{u}(X) is not far from calibration.

3.2 Measuring UC⁡(f,u)\mathrm{UC}\left(f,u\right)

A naturally arising question is on the difficulty of measuring and achieving a small utility calibration error. We show in Lemma 3.3 that both the computational and sample complexity of estimating UC⁡(f,u)\mathrm{UC}\left(f,u\right) are generally feasible and of limited dependence on the dimension, allowing its scalability to predictors with thousands of classes.

Lemma 3.3 (Estimating Utility Calibration Against a Single Function).

Let u:ΔC−1×𝒴→[−1,1]u:\Delta^{C-1}\times\mathcal{Y}\rightarrow[-1,1] be a fixed utility function and f:𝒳→ΔC−1f:\mathcal{X}\to\Delta^{C-1} be a given predictor. Define the empirical estimator UC^​(f,u,S)\widehat{\mathrm{UC}}(f,u;S) based on nn i.i.d. samples S={(Xi,Yi)}i=1n∼DnS=\{(X_{i},Y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n}\sim D^{n} as

supI∈𝕀⁡[−1,1]|1n​∑i=1n[(u⁡(f⁡(Xi),Yi)−vu​(Xi))​𝟙vu​(Xi)∈I]|.\displaystyle\sup_{{I\in\mathbb{I}\left[-1,1\right]}}\Big|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\big[{(u(f(X_{i}),Y_{i})-v_{u}(X_{i}))}\mathbbm{1}_{v_{u}(X_{i})\in I}\big]\Big|.

Then, for any δ>0\delta>0, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta over the draws of the sample SS,

|UC^​(f,u,S)−UC⁡(f,u)|≤O~​(log⁡(1/δ)n).\textstyle|\widehat{\mathrm{UC}}(f,u;S)-\mathrm{UC}(f,u)|\leq\tilde{O}\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{n}}\right). (3.4)

Furthermore, UC^​(f,u,S)\widehat{\mathrm{UC}}(f,u;S) can be computed from SS in O⁡(n​log⁡(n)+n​Te​v​a​l)O(n\log(n)+nT_{eval}) time, where Te​v​a​lT_{eval} is the time to evaluate f⁡(Xi)f(X_{i}) and u⁡(⋅,⋅)u(\cdot,\cdot).

First, we note that the constants hidden in the O~​(⋅)\tilde{O}(\cdot) in (3.4) are dimension-independent. Similarly, the only dimension-dependent term in the computational complexity is Te​v​a​lT_{eval}. As such, UC⁡(f,u)\mathrm{UC}\left(f,u\right) is a completely scalable notion of calibration, allowing it to be implemented for classifiers with a thousand classes – as exemplified in Section 5. In addition, given that UC⁡(f,u)\mathrm{UC}(f,u) can be formulated as weighted calibration (see eq. (3.3)) and that UC^​(f,u,S)\widehat{\mathrm{UC}}(f,u;S) is both computationally and sample efficient, we can leverage standard patching-style post-hoc calibration (Jung et al., 2021; Hébert-Johnson et al., 2018; Duchi, 2024) to recalibrate ff so as to minimize UC⁡(f,u)\mathrm{UC}\left(f,u\right) while decreasing its Brier score. Concretely, the recalibrator iteratively identifies worst-interval witnesses for uu and applies corrections to f⁡(X)f(X) that reduce the utility calibration error and the Brier score; see Appendix A for a detailed description and Appendix C for implementational details and experiments. With these encouraging facts on the utility calibration w.r.t. a single uu being established, we next turn our attention to Utility Calibration against a function class 𝒰\mathcal{U}.

3.3 Utility calibration against a function class

In many real-world scenarios, a single probabilistic predictor ff might serve multiple downstream users, or a single user might employ it under varying conditions or objectives. The exact utility function relevant at the time of decision-making may not be known beforehand, or it might even change over time (e.g., due to changing costs, available actions, or strategic goals), or it might be fundamentally user-dependent.

Therefore, ensuring reliability often requires guarantees that hold not just for a single, pre-specified utility function, but for an entire class of plausible or relevant utility functions, denoted by 𝒰{\cal U}. This provides a more robust assurance that the model’s predictions are trustworthy across a range of potential downstream applications. To capture this requirement, overloading the notation, we define utility calibration against a function class as the worst-case performance over the class, i.e.

UC⁡(f,𝒰)=supu∈𝒰UC⁡(f,u).\mathrm{UC}\left(f,{\cal U}\right)=\sup_{u\in{\cal U}}\mathrm{UC}\left(f,u\right). (3.5)

To illustrate the practical relevance of this concept, we exhibit hereafter several examples of utility classes, each motivated by different downstream tasks. We first demonstrate how to recover similar notions to top-class (2.1) and class-wise (2.2) using the framework of utility calibration (3.5).

Example 3.4 (Top-Class and Class-Wise Utilities (𝒰TCE,𝒰CWE{\cal U}_{\mathrm{TCE}},{\cal U}_{\mathrm{CWE}})).

Again using the shorthands fi≔f​(X)if_{i}\coloneqq f(X)_{i}, p∗≔f​(X)i∗p_{*}\coloneq f(X)_{i_{*}}, and Y∗≔𝟙Y=ei∗Y_{*}\coloneq\mathbbm{1}_{Y=e_{i_{*}}}, where i∗≔argmaxi​f​(X)ii_{*}\coloneq\mathrm{argmax}_{i}f(X)_{i}, define

UC⁡(f,𝒰TCE)\displaystyle\mathrm{UC}(f,{\cal U}_{\mathrm{TCE}}) =supI⊆[0,1]|𝔼[(Y∗−p∗)​𝟙p∗∈I]|,\displaystyle=\sup_{I\subseteq[0,1]}|\expec[(Y_{*}-p_{*})\mathbbm{1}_{p_{*}\in I}]|,
UC⁡(f,𝒰CWE)\displaystyle\mathrm{UC}(f,{\cal U}_{\mathrm{CWE}}) =supc∈[C],I⊆[0,1]|𝔼[(𝟙Y=ec−f​(X)c)​𝟙f​(X)c∈I]|.\displaystyle=\sup_{\mathclap{c\in[C],I\subseteq[0,1]}}|\expec[(\mathbbm{1}_{Y=e_{c}}-f(X)_{c})\mathbbm{1}_{f(X)_{c}\in I}]|.

In contrast to the binned estimators TCEbin\mathrm{TCE}^{\mathrm{bin}} (2.1) and CWEbin\mathrm{CWE}^{\mathrm{bin}} (2.2), utility calibration with the classes 𝒰TCE{\cal U}_{\mathrm{TCE}} and 𝒰CWE{\cal U}_{\mathrm{CWE}} offers a more robust, binning-free, computable assessment. Specifically, UC⁡(f,𝒰TCE)\mathrm{UC}\left(f,{\cal U}_{\mathrm{TCE}}\right) and UC⁡(f,𝒰CWE)\mathrm{UC}\left(f,{\cal U}_{\mathrm{CWE}}\right) are determined by maximizing the calibration deviation over any possible interval I⊆[0,1]I\subseteq[0,1] (and additionally over classes for 𝒰CWE{\cal U}_{\mathrm{CWE}}), effectively identifying the worst-case interval-based error. This approach inherently avoids fixed binning schemes, thereby circumventing pathologies where bin choices drastically alter estimated errors (Roelofs et al., 2022; Kumar et al., 2019). Consequently, for any binning scheme using mm bins, m⋅UC⁡(f,𝒰TCE)m\cdot\mathrm{UC}\left(f,{\cal U}_{\mathrm{TCE}}\right) and m⋅UC⁡(f,𝒰CWE)m\cdot\mathrm{UC}\left(f,{\cal U}_{\mathrm{CWE}}\right) upper bound TCEbin​(f)\mathrm{TCE}^{\mathrm{bin}}(f) and CWEbin​(f)\mathrm{CWE}^{\mathrm{bin}}(f) respectively, while the converse is not true. We refer to Appendix B.2 for the formal statement. Furthermore, by Proposition 3.1, a small UC⁡(f,𝒰TCE)\mathrm{UC}\left(f,{\cal U}_{\mathrm{TCE}}\right) guarantees that decisions based on thresholding top-class confidence are robust to monotonic recalibration, and by Proposition 3.2 that this confidence is a calibrated predictor of actual top-class accuracy. Analogous guarantees hold for UC⁡(f,𝒰CWE)\mathrm{UC}\left(f,{\cal U}_{\mathrm{CWE}}\right) for individual class confidences, offering assurances for downstream applications.

Beyond the binarized perspectives offered by 𝒰TCE{\cal U}_{\mathrm{TCE}} and 𝒰CWE{\cal U}_{\mathrm{CWE}}, the utility calibration framework readily accommodates richer and more complex classes of utility functions. This allows us to move beyond presumptive binary events and consider more nuanced downstream applications. In particular, consider settings where the utility derived from an outcome YY is intrinsic to the outcome itself, independent of the model’s prediction f⁡(X)f(X). For example, in medical diagnosis, the cost or severity tied to a specific disease Y=ejY=e_{j} might be a fixed value aja_{j}, irrespective of the diagnostic prediction. Formally, such situations can be modeled using a utility function ua:ΔC−1×𝒴→[−1,1]u_{a}:\Delta^{C-1}\times\mathcal{Y}\to[-1,1] defined by a payoff vector a∈[−1,1]Ca\in[-1,1]^{C}, where the utility function and the expected utility are respectively ua​(⋅,ej)=aju_{a}(\cdot,e_{j})=a_{j} and vua​(X)=⟨f⁡(X),a⟩v_{u_{a}}(X)=\left\langle f(X),a\right\rangle, with aja_{j} representing the utility if the true outcome is eje_{j}.

Example 3.5 (Linear Utilities (𝒰lin{\cal U}_{\mathrm{lin}})).

Define the class of linear utilities as 𝒰lin≔{ua∣a∈[−1,1]C}{\cal U}_{\mathrm{lin}}\coloneqq\{u_{a}\mid a\in[-1,1]^{C}\}, noting that the predicted utility vua​(X)v_{u_{a}}(X) is linear in the prediction f⁡(X)f(X).

A small UC⁡(f,𝒰lin)\mathrm{UC}(f,{\cal U}_{\mathrm{lin}}) ensures that for any payoff vector aa, the predicted expected utility vua​(X)v_{u_{a}}(X), as a regressor of the realized utility, is close to calibration.

Alternatively, in applications like information retrieval or recommender systems, the realized utility depends on the rank assigned to the true outcome Y=ejY=e_{j}. Given a model’s prediction p=f⁡(X)p=f(X), assuming p1,…,pCp_{1},\ldots,p_{C} are distinct (or that ties are broken arbitrarily/randomly among equal coordinates), the rank of class jj, denoted rank⁡(p,j)\mathrm{rank}(p,j), is its position across pp, i.e. rank(p,j)≔∑i∈[C]𝟙{pj≤pi}\mathrm{rank}(p,j)\coloneqq\sum_{i\in[C]}\mathbbm{1}\left\{p_{j}\leq p_{i}\right\}. Using a valuation vector θ∈[−1,1]C\theta\in[-1,1]^{C}, a rank-based utility function can then be constructed as uθ​(p,ej)=θrank⁡(p,j)u_{\theta}(p,e_{j})=\theta_{\mathrm{rank}(p,j)} with the associated expected utility function vuθ​(X)=∑i=1Cf​(X)i​θrank⁡(f⁡(X),i)v_{u_{\theta}}(X)=\sum_{i=1}^{C}f(X)_{i}\theta_{\mathrm{rank}(f(X),i)}. Calibrating for such utilities ensures the model’s expected rank-based performance aligns with reality. A prominent special case is topK\mathrm{topK} utility, where the valuation vector θ(K)\theta^{(K)} for a given K∈[C]K\in[C] is defined such that θr(K)=1\theta^{(K)}_{r}=1 if r≤Kr\leq K and θr(K)=0\theta^{(K)}_{r}=0 if r>Kr>K.

Example 3.6 (Rank-Based and Top-KK Utilities (𝒰rank,𝒰topK{\cal U}_{\mathrm{rank}},{\cal U}_{\mathrm{topK}})).

The class of general rank-based utilities is 𝒰rank≔{uθ∣θ∈[−1,1]C}{\cal U}_{\mathrm{rank}}\coloneqq\{u_{\theta}\mid\theta\in[-1,1]^{C}\}. The class of top-KK utilities is then 𝒰topK≔{uθ(K)∣K∈[C]}{\cal U}_{\mathrm{topK}}\coloneqq\{u_{\theta^{(K)}}\mid K\in[C]\}, where θr(K)=𝟙{r≤K}\theta^{(K)}_{r}=\mathbbm{1}\{r\leq K\}. Equivalently, uK(p,ej)=𝟙{rank(p,j)≤K}u_{K}(p,e_{j})=\mathbbm{1}\{\mathrm{rank}(p,j)\leq K\}. A small UC⁡(f,𝒰rank)\mathrm{UC}(f,{\cal U}_{\mathrm{rank}}) (or UC⁡(f,𝒰topK𝐶𝐿𝑂𝑆𝐸\mathrm{UC}(f,{\cal U}_{\mathrm{topK}})) ensures reliable prediction for general rank (or specifically top-KK accuracy) valuations, validating the model’s ranking capabilities.

As discussed in Section 2, decision calibration (Zhao et al., 2021) ensures that for problems with up to KK actions, the model’s predicted utility for its recommended action matches the actual realized utility. We can frame a similar guarantee within utility calibration. For any bounded loss function l:𝒴×[K]→[−1,1]l:\mathcal{Y}\times[K]\to[-1,1] and a prediction p=f⁡(X)p=f(X), the optimal action is δl​(p)=arg⁡mina∈[K]​𝔼Y^∼p​[l⁡(Y^,a)]\delta_{l}(p)=\arg\min_{a\in[K]}\mathbb{E}_{\hat{Y}\sim p}[l(\hat{Y},a)]. The utility function is then ul​(p,y)=−l⁡(y,δl​(p))u_{l}(p,y)=-l(y,\delta_{l}(p)), representing the negative loss from outcome yy under action δl​(p)\delta_{l}(p). The predicted expected utility is vul​(X)=−𝔼Y^∼f⁡(X)​[l⁡(Y^,δl​(f⁡(X)))|X]v_{u_{l}}(X)=-\mathbb{E}_{\hat{Y}\sim f(X)}[l(\hat{Y},\delta_{l}(f(X)))|X].

Example 3.7 (Decision Calibration Utilities (𝒰dec,K{\cal U}_{\mathrm{dec},K})).

Let ℒK={l:𝒴×[K]→[−1,1]}\mathcal{L}_{K}=\{l:\mathcal{Y}\times[K]\to[-1,1]\} be the class of all bounded KK-action loss functions, and the utility class is 𝒰dec,K≔{ul,l∈ℒK}{\cal U}_{\mathrm{dec},K}\coloneqq\{u_{l},l\in\mathcal{L}_{K}\}. A small UC⁡(f,𝒰dec,K)\mathrm{UC}(f,{\cal U}_{\mathrm{dec},K}) implies that for any KK-action decision problem l∈ℒKl\in\mathcal{L}_{K}, the model’s prediction of expected utility for its chosen action δl​(f​(X))\delta_{l}(f(X)) reliably reflects the achieved utility −l⁡(Y,δl​(f⁡(X)))-l(Y,\delta_{l}(f(X))).

These aforementioned examples illustrate that calibrating against classes 𝒰{\cal U} provides guarantees tailored to diverse user needs, moving beyond simplistic binarized assessments. A critical question then arises: how can UC⁡(f,𝒰)\mathrm{UC}\left(f,{\cal U}\right) be measured for a given class 𝒰{\cal U}, which we address in the next section.

4 SCALABLE EVALUATION OF UTILITY CALIBRATION

Estimating supu∈𝒰UC⁡(f,u)\sup_{u\in{\cal U}}\mathrm{UC}\left(f,u\right) in (3.5) presents two key challenges: the computational complexity of the optimization, and the sample complexity required for the empirical supremum to converge to its true value. We introduce the two notions of proactive and interactive measurability to decouple these two aspects.

Definition 4.1 (Proactive Measurability).

The utility calibration error w.r.t. class 𝒰{\cal U} is proactively measurable if there exists an algorithm AA and polynomial functions Np​o​l​y,Tp​o​l​yN_{poly},T_{poly} such that for any ε,δ>0\varepsilon,\delta>0 and n≥Np​o​l​y​(C,1/ε,1/δ)n\geq N_{poly}(C,1/\varepsilon,1/\delta) samples S∼DnS\sim D^{n}, algorithm A⁡(S)A(S) outputs u^\hat{u} satisfying |UC⁡(f,u^)−UC⁡(f,𝒰)|≤ε|\mathrm{UC}\left(f,\hat{u}\right)-\mathrm{UC}\left(f,{\cal U}\right)|\leq\varepsilon with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta and the runtime of A⁡(S)A(S) is bounded by Tp​o​l​y​(C,n)T_{poly}(C,n).

Generally, for a finite class 𝒰{\cal U}, if |𝒰|\left\lvert{\cal U}\right\rvert grows polynomially in CC then by Lemma 3.3 we can guarantee proactive measurability. Nonetheless, even for simple infinite classes such as 𝒰lin{\cal U}_{\mathrm{lin}}, proactive measurability reduces to a non-convex optimization problem that cannot be generally solved in polynomial time. In fact, even aiming for a weaker notion, namely improper auditing, Gopalan et al. (2024) showed that assessing both weaker and stronger notions than UC⁡(f,𝒰lin)\mathrm{UC}\left(f,{\cal U}_{\mathrm{lin}}\right) cannot be done in polynomial time in both the error ε−1{\varepsilon}^{-1} and the dimension CC (Gopalan et al., 2024, Theorem 1.3, Theorem 5.2, and Theorem 8.6). A more detailed description of Gopalan et al. (2024) hardness results is in Section B.3. Next, we thus propose an alternative criterion of measurability that decouples the statistical guarantee from the computational complexity of verifying the supremum.

Definition 4.2 (Interactive Measurability).

The utility calibration error w.r.t. class 𝒰{\cal U} is interactively measurable if there exists an estimator UC^​(f,u,S)\widehat{\mathrm{UC}}(f,u;S) and a polynomial function Np​o​l​yN_{poly} such that for n≥Np​o​l​y​(C,1/ε,1/δ)n\geq N_{poly}(C,1/\varepsilon,1/\delta) samples S∼DnS\sim D^{n}, it holds with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta that supu∈𝒰|UC^​(f,u,S)−UC⁡(f,u)|≤ε\textstyle\sup_{u\in{\cal U}}|\widehat{\mathrm{UC}}(f,u;S)-\mathrm{UC}(f,u)|\leq\varepsilon.

Interactive measurability represents a much more achievable goal. For example, while decision calibration is computationally hard to measure, Zhao et al. (2021) showed that it admits polynomial sample complexity. In Appendix B.4, we prove the interactive measurability of 𝒰lin{\cal U}_{\mathrm{lin}} and 𝒰rank{\cal U}_{\mathrm{rank}} and that for both the sample complexity if O~​(C)\tilde{O}(C). In addition, we demonstrate that for a class of utilities 𝒰{\cal U}, it is interactively measurable if the functions of the form f⁡(X)→u⁡(f⁡(X),ei)​𝟙vu​(X)∈If(X)\rightarrow u(f(X),e_{i})\mathbbm{1}_{v_{u}(X)\in I} for u∈𝒰u\in{\cal U}, i∈[C]i\in[C], and I∈𝕀⁡[−1,1]I\in\mathbb{I}\left[-1,1\right] admit a controlled Rademacher complexity.

In summary, while proactively measuring the worst-case utility calibration error UC⁡(f,𝒰)=supu∈𝒰UC⁡(f,u)\mathrm{UC}(f,{\cal U})=\sup_{u\in{\cal U}}\mathrm{UC}(f,u) is often computationally prohibitive for expressive utility classes 𝒰{\cal U}, interactive measurability allows for efficient estimation of UC⁡(f,u)\mathrm{UC}(f,u) uniformly for any specific u∈𝒰u\in{\cal U}. Next, we leverage this distinction to propose a scalable evaluation methodology that, instead of pursuing the intractable worst-case error, characterizes the distribution of utility calibration errors across 𝒰{\cal U}. This provides a more nuanced understanding of a model ff’s calibration reliability over a spectrum of potential downstream applications, that we then evaluate in experiments.

Our approach considers a probability distribution 𝒟𝒰\mathcal{D}_{{\cal U}} over the utility class 𝒰{\cal U}. Many utility classes of interest admit a finite-dimensional parameterization, making sampling from 𝒟𝒰\mathcal{D}_{{\cal U}} practical. We sample MM utility functions {um}m=1M\{u_{m}\}_{m=1}^{M} from 𝒟𝒰\mathcal{D}_{{\cal U}} and, for each umu_{m}, compute its estimated error E^m,n≔UC^​(f,um,S)\widehat{E}_{m,n}\coloneqq\widehat{\mathrm{UC}}(f,u_{m};S) using nn data points from a sample SS. These MM error estimates then form an empirical Cumulative Distribution Function (eCDF), F^E,M,n(e)≔1M∑m=1M𝟙{E^m,n≤e}\textstyle\widehat{F}_{E,M,n}(e)\coloneqq\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\mathbbm{1}\{\widehat{E}_{m,n}\leq e\}, which serves as an empirical proxy for the true CDF, FE​(e)≔ℙu∼𝒟𝒰(UC⁡(f,u)≤e)F_{E}(e)\coloneqq\prob_{u\sim\mathcal{D}_{{\cal U}}}(\mathrm{UC}(f,u)\leq e). We provide guarantees on the difference between FE​(e)F_{E}(e) and F^E,M,n​(e)\hat{F}_{E,M,n}(e) in Appendix B.5. Informally, if individual utility-calibration errors can be uniformly estimated to accuracy εstat\varepsilon_{\text{stat}} from nn samples, then with high probability over the draw of the dataset and the MM sampled utilities, the deviation between the true CDF FEF_{E} and the empirical eCDF F^E,M,n\widehat{F}_{E,M,n} in L2L_{2} scales as O~​(εstat+1M)\tilde{O}\!\left(\sqrt{\varepsilon_{\text{stat}}}+\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{M}}\right).

In particular, 𝒰lin{\cal U}_{\mathrm{lin}} (Example 3.5) and 𝒰rank{\cal U}_{\mathrm{rank}} (Example 3.6) both admit finite-dimension parameterization. For 𝒰lin{\cal U}_{\mathrm{lin}}, we construct 𝒟𝒰lin{\mathcal{D}}_{{\cal U}_{\mathrm{lin}}} by sampling the payoff vectors aa uniformly in ∂B∞≔{a∈ℝC:‖a‖∞=1}\partial B_{\infty}\coloneq\left\{a\in\mathbb{R}^{C}:\left\lVert a\right\rVert_{\infty}=1\right\}. Meanwhile, for 𝒰rank{\cal U}_{\mathrm{rank}}, we also sample from 𝒟𝒰rank{\mathcal{D}}_{{\cal U}_{\mathrm{rank}}} by uniformly sampling valuation vectors ∂B∞\partial B_{\infty}, which satisfy θ1≥θ2≥⋯≥θC\theta_{1}\geq\theta_{2}\geq\dots\geq\theta_{C}. This is to reflect a rational preference for better ranks, i.e. the higher the rank of the true realization within the predictions of f⁡(X)f(X), the higher the utility.

5 EXPERIMENTS

We now demonstrate our evaluation on ImageNet-1K (Deng et al., 2009) with a pretrained Vision Transformer (ViT) (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021). We compare the calibration performance of Temperature Scaling (Temp. Scaling) (Platt et al., 1999), Vector Scaling (Kull et al., 2017), Dirichlet recalibration (Kull et al., 2019), and Isotonic Regression (I.R.) (Zadrozny and Elkan, 2002). In addition, we use a simple auditing/patching-style post-hoc calibration algorithm inspired by previous work (Hébert-Johnson et al., 2018; Jung et al., 2021). In summary, this patching algorithm iteratively evaluates the utility calibration on the class 𝒰comb\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{comb}}, which combines class-wise and top-KK utilities, i.e., 𝒰comb≔𝒰CWE∪𝒰topK{\cal U}_{\mathrm{comb}}\coloneqq{\cal U}_{\mathrm{CWE}}\cup{\cal U}_{\mathrm{topK}}. Then, the algorithm patches the pretrained predictor ff to improve the utility calibration error against the class 𝒰comb{\cal U}_{\mathrm{comb}}. We provide a detailed description of the algorithm and our implementation in Appendices A&C.

Moreover, Appendix C provides extended results: additional architectures, datasets, and modalities, sensitivity to aligned vs. misaligned utilities, and additional commonly used utility families such as discounted cumulative gain (Järvelin and Kekäläinen, 2002) and hierarchical classification loss (Deng et al., 2012). These experiments further illustrate the advantages of our framework and the failure modes of traditional metrics.

In Table 1, we compare Brier score, binned binarized metrics TCEbinned\mathrm{TCE}_{\mathrm{binned}} and CWEbinned\mathrm{CWE}_{\mathrm{binned}} (with 1515 equal-weight bins), and a combined utility calibration metric w.r.t. the class 𝒰comb\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{comb}}. We note that, given that both 𝒰CWE{\cal U}_{\mathrm{CWE}} and 𝒰topK{\cal U}_{\mathrm{topK}} are finite classes, 𝒰comb\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{comb}} can be directly measured with no sampling required. As expected, all post-hoc methods improve Brier and calibration errors. Nonetheless, no single method performed the best uniformly across all metrics. We note that the patching-style post-hoc calibration achieves the best top-class binned calibration error and 𝒰comb\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{comb}}.

Beyond specific utility functions, Figure 1 displays eCDFs of utility calibration errors for broader utility classes: rank-based (𝒰rank{\cal U}_{\mathrm{rank}}) and linear (𝒰lin{\cal U}_{\mathrm{lin}}). For utility sampling, we used the approach described in Section 4. Each eCDF (from M=1500M{=}1500 sampled utilities) shows the proportion of utilities with error below a threshold; curves further left indicate better calibration across the class. On ViT-ImageNet-1K, the uncalibrated model is consistently worst across both classes, while post-hoc methods shift the curves left to varying degrees, revealing method-dependent tradeoffs. Interestingly, the eCDF curves surface trends that the aggregate scores in Table 1 can obscure: for example, how tightly errors concentrate around the median, and whether heavy tails persist, even when summary metrics look similar. In addition, performance is not uniform across utility families: some methods yield larger gains on 𝒰lin{\cal U}_{\mathrm{lin}} while others help more on 𝒰rank{\cal U}_{\mathrm{rank}}, underscoring the importance of matching the calibrator to the target utility class. For example, while Vector Scaling performed the best on 𝒰rank{\cal U}_{\mathrm{rank}}, it performed the worst on 𝒰lin{\cal U}_{\mathrm{lin}}.

In conclusion, utility calibration provides a robust, unified, and application-centric framework for evaluating classifier reliability. Its specific instantiations, 𝒰CWE{\cal U}_{\mathrm{CWE}} and 𝒰TCE{\cal U}_{\mathrm{TCE}}, offer superior, binning-free alternatives to traditional metrics with actionable guarantees. Furthermore, the eCDF plots across broader utility classes deliver crucial nuanced insights into model behavior that single-metric evaluations obscure.

Scalable Utility-Aware Multiclass Calibration:
Supplementary Materials

 

Organization of the Appendix

The appendix is organized as follows: Appendix A presents the post-hoc patching algorithm for utility calibration; Appendix B collects deferred material, including CutOff calibration (Section B.1), bounds for binned estimators (Section B.2), computational aspects of proactive measurability (Section B.3), sample complexity bounds for interactive measurability (Section B.4), and eCDF guarantees (Section B.5). Then, Section B.6 presents proofs of statements that were explicitly stated in the main body. Finally, Appendix C provides additional experiments.

Appendix Contents

Appendix A Post-Hoc Patching Algorithm for Utility Calibration

This section details a post-hoc calibration algorithm aimed at reducing the utility calibration error UC⁡(f,𝒰)\mathrm{UC}(f,{\cal U}) with respect to a specific utility function class 𝒰{\cal U}. As established in the main text (eq. 3.3), utility calibration can be cast as a form of weighted calibration. Recall that for a single uu,

UC⁡(f,u)=supw∈𝒲⁡(u)𝔼⁡[⟨f⁡(X)−Y,w⁡(f⁡(X))⟩],\displaystyle\mathrm{UC}\left(f,u\right)=\sup_{w\in\mathcal{W}(u)}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\langle f(X)-Y,w(f(X))\right\rangle\right],

where 𝒲(u)={x→ξu→(X)𝟙{vu(X)∈I}|I∈𝕀[−1,1],ξ∈{−1,1}}\mathcal{W}(u)=\left\{x\rightarrow\xi\vec{u}(X)\mathbbm{1}\left\{v_{u}(X)\in I\right\}|I\in\mathbb{I}\left[-1,1\right],\xi\in\left\{-1,1\right\}\right\}. This naturally extends to a utility function class 𝒰{\cal U} by defining 𝒲(𝒰)=∪u∈𝒰𝒲(u)\mathcal{W}({\cal U})=\cup_{u\in{\cal U}}\mathcal{W}\left(u\right). Then it holds that UC⁡(f,𝒰)=CE𝒲⁡(𝒰)​(f)\mathrm{UC}\left(f,{\cal U}\right)=\mathrm{CE}_{\mathcal{W}\left({\cal U}\right)}\left(f\right).

Given that utility calibration can be cast as weighted calibration, algorithms from the literature can be used to post-hoc calibrate ff such that it has a small utility calibration error. In particular, Algorithm 1 iteratively finds the worst witness w∈𝒲⁡(𝒰)w\in\mathcal{W}\left({\cal U}\right) and adjusts the predictor ff to correct for this specific violation. This approach is common in (multi)calibration literature, for example (Hébert-Johnson et al., 2018; Gopalan et al., 2022a; Jung et al., 2021), a more general version is presented in (Duchi, 2024, Chapter 15). A key property is that these adjustments can be made such that the model’s Brier score decreases in every iteration.

Here πΔC−1\pi_{\Delta^{C-1}} is the projection onto the simplex and ηt\eta_{t} is a possibly adaptive stepsize.

Proposition A.1 (Convergence and Brier Score Guarantee).

Assume oracle access to compute errt\mathrm{err}_{t} and the corresponding witness wt∈𝒲⁡(𝒰)w_{t}\in\mathcal{W}\left({\cal U}\right) at each iteration tt. Let CC be the number of classes. With the stepsize ηt=errt/C\eta_{t}=\mathrm{err}_{t}/C, Algorithm 1 terminates in T=O⁡(C/ε2)T=O(C/\varepsilon^{2}) iterations

Proof.

We include the proof for completeness. It follows the approach of Hébert-Johnson et al. (2018) in using the Brier score as a potential function and showing that it monotonically decreases across iterations. It is the same as the version in Gopalan et al. (2024). A more general version can be found in Duchi (2024, Chapter 15). The change in Brier score L⁡(f)=𝔼⁡[‖Y−f⁡(X)‖22]L(f)=\mathbb{E}[\|Y-f(X)\|_{2}^{2}] from f(t)f^{(t)} to f(t+1)f^{(t+1)} is:

L⁡(f(t+1))−L⁡(f(t))\displaystyle L(f^{(t+1)})-L(f^{(t)}) ≤𝔼⁡[‖Y−(f(t)​(X)−ηt​wt​(f(t)​(X)))‖22−‖Y−f(t)​(X)‖22]\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}\left[\|Y-(f^{(t)}(X)-\eta_{t}w_{t}(f^{(t)}(X)))\|_{2}^{2}-\|Y-f^{(t)}(X)\|_{2}^{2}\right]
=𝔼⁡[2​ηt​⟨Y−f(t)​(X),wt​(f(t)​(X))⟩+ηt2​‖wt​(f(t)​(X))‖22]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[2\eta_{t}\left\langle Y-f^{(t)}(X),w_{t}(f^{(t)}(X))\right\rangle+\eta_{t}^{2}\|w_{t}(f^{(t)}(X))\|_{2}^{2}\right]
=𝔼⁡[−2​ηt​⟨f(t)​(X)−Y,wt​(f(t)​(X))⟩+ηt2​‖wt​(f(t)​(X))‖22]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[-2\eta_{t}\left\langle f^{(t)}(X)-Y,w_{t}(f^{(t)}(X))\right\rangle+\eta_{t}^{2}\|w_{t}(f^{(t)}(X))\|_{2}^{2}\right]
=−2​ηt​errt+ηt2​𝔼​[‖wt​(f(t)​(X))‖22].\displaystyle=-2\eta_{t}\text{err}_{t}+\eta_{t}^{2}\mathbb{E}[\|w_{t}(f^{(t)}(X))\|_{2}^{2}].

Each witness w∈𝒲⁡(𝒰)w\in\mathcal{W}({\cal U}) is of the form p↦ξu→(p)𝟙{vu(p)∈I}p\mapsto\xi\vec{u}(p)\mathbbm{1}\{v_{u}(p)\in I\} for ξ∈{−1,1}\xi\in\left\{-1,1\right\} and u∈𝒰u\in{\cal U}. Since u⁡(⋅,ej)∈[−1,1]u(\cdot,e_{j})\in[-1,1], ‖u→​(p)‖22≤‖u→​(p)‖∞​‖u→​(p)‖1≤C\|\vec{u}(p)\|_{2}^{2}\leq\left\lVert\vec{u}(p)\right\rVert_{\infty}\left\lVert\vec{u}(p)\right\rVert_{1}\leq C. Thus, ‖wt​(p)‖22≤C\|w_{t}(p)\|_{2}^{2}\leq C. Substituting ηt=errt/C\eta_{t}=\text{err}_{t}/C:

L⁡(f(t+1))−L⁡(f(t))\displaystyle L(f^{(t+1)})-L(f^{(t)}) ≤−2​errtC​errt+(errtC)2​𝔼​[‖wt​(f(t)​(X))‖22]\displaystyle\leq-2\frac{\text{err}_{t}}{C}\text{err}_{t}+\left(\frac{\text{err}_{t}}{C}\right)^{2}\mathbb{E}[\|w_{t}(f^{(t)}(X))\|_{2}^{2}]
≤−2​errt2C+errt2​CC2=−errt2C.\displaystyle\leq-\frac{2\text{err}_{t}^{2}}{C}+\frac{\text{err}_{t}^{2}C}{C^{2}}=-\frac{\text{err}_{t}^{2}}{C}.

This proves that the Brier score does not increase and strictly decreases if errt>0\text{err}_{t}>0. If the algorithm continues, it is because errt>ε\text{err}_{t}>\varepsilon, so the decrease is at least ε2/C\varepsilon^{2}/C. Since L⁡(f)∈[0,2]L(f)\in[0,2] (as ‖Y−f⁡(X)‖22≤‖Y‖22+‖f⁡(X)‖22≤1+1=2\|Y-f(X)\|_{2}^{2}\leq\|Y\|_{2}^{2}+\|f(X)\|_{2}^{2}\leq 1+1=2), and at step errt>ε\text{err}_{t}>\varepsilon decreases L⁡(f)L(f) by at least ε2/C\varepsilon^{2}/C, the algorithm must terminate in at most O⁡(C/ε2)O\left(C/\varepsilon^{2}\right) such steps. ∎

Empirical Implementation and Sample Complexity.

In practice, direct computation of expectations within Algorithm 1 is infeasible. Instead, the algorithm is implemented using a dataset StS^{t} of NN i.i.d. samples at each iteration tt. Both the maximization step to find the witness wtw_{t} and the computation of the error errt\text{err}_{t} are performed using empirical averages 𝔼^N​[⋅]\hat{\mathbb{E}}_{N}[\cdot] over StS^{t}.

The theoretical convergence guarantees of Proposition A.1 (i.e., termination in O⁡(C/ε2)O(C/\varepsilon^{2}) iterations) can be extended to this empirical setting, provided that the empirically estimated error err^t≔𝔼^N​[⟨f(t)​(X)−Y,wt​(X)⟩]\widehat{\text{err}}_{t}\coloneqq\hat{\mathbb{E}}_{N}[\left\langle f^{(t)}(X)-Y,w_{t}(X)\right\rangle] is a sufficiently accurate approximation of the true error errt\text{err}_{t}. Specifically, if err^t\widehat{\text{err}}_{t} is within O⁡(ε)O(\varepsilon) of errt\text{err}_{t} whenever errt>ε\text{err}_{t}>\varepsilon, the iteration complexity remains O⁡(C/ε2)O(C/\varepsilon^{2}).

The number of samples NN required per iteration to achieve an O⁡(ε)O(\varepsilon)-accurate estimation of errt\text{err}_{t}, with probability 1−δ1-\delta, depends on the complexity of the witness class 𝒲⁡(𝒰)\mathcal{W}({\cal U}). For the Top-Class utility 𝒰TCE{\cal U}_{\mathrm{TCE}}, where |𝒰|=1|\mathcal{U}|=1, using Lemma 3.3, N≤O~​(log⁡(1/δ)ε2)N\leq\tilde{O}\left(\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{\varepsilon^{2}}\right). Similarly, Class-Wise utility 𝒰CWE{\cal U}_{\mathrm{CWE}} and Top-K utility 𝒰topK{\cal U}_{\mathrm{topK}}, where for both |𝒰|=C|\mathcal{U}|=C, using a simple union bound, we recover N≤O~​(log⁡(C/δ)ε2)N\leq\tilde{O}\left(\frac{\log(C/\delta)}{\varepsilon^{2}}\right).

Appendix B Deferred Content

B.1 CutOff Calibration

In Section 3, we highlighted that our utility calibration framework, particularly its focus on worst-case interval-based deviations of predicted utility, can be seen as a natural extension of the binary CutOff calibration concept to multiclass scenarios and general utility functions. This extension preserves important decision-theoretic properties. For the binary setting (Y∈{0,1},f:𝒳→[0,1]Y\in\{0,1\},f:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow[0,1]), Rossellini et al. (2025) demonstrate that if the metric

ΔCutoff(f)≔supI∈𝕀⁡[0,1]|𝔼[(Y−f(X))𝟙{f(X)∈I}]|\Delta_{\operatorname{Cutoff}}(f)\coloneqq\sup_{I\in\mathbb{I}\left[0,1\right]}|\mathbb{E}[(Y-f(X))\mathbbm{1}\left\{f(X)\in I\right\}]|

is small, then a simple decision rule Y^τ:X→{0,1}\widehat{Y}_{\tau}:X\rightarrow\left\{0,1\right\} of the form Y^τ=𝟙{f(X)≥τ}\hat{Y}_{\tau}=\mathbbm{1}\left\{f(X)\geq\tau\right\} evaluated against its associated binary decision loss, cannot be substantially improved by monotonic post-hoc calibration. More concretely, let Rbd​(g,τ):=𝔼⁡[ℓbd​(Y,Y^τ,τ)]R_{\mathrm{bd}}(g;\tau):=\mathbb{E}[\ell_{\mathrm{bd}}(Y,\hat{Y}_{\tau};\tau)] be the risk under the binary decision loss ℓbd​(Y,Y^,τ)=τ⁡(1−Y)​Y^+(1−τ)​Y​(1−Y^)\ell_{\mathrm{bd}}(Y,\widehat{Y};\tau)=\tau(1-Y)\widehat{Y}+(1-\tau)Y(1-\widehat{Y}). Then, Rossellini et al. (2025, Prop. 3.2) show that for any τ∈[0,1]\tau\in[0,1]:

Rbd(f;τ)−infh:[0,1]→[0,1]monotoneRbd(h∘f;τ)≤ 2ΔCutoff(f).\displaystyle R_{\mathrm{bd}}(f;\tau)-\inf_{\begin{subarray}{c}h:[0,1]\rightarrow[0,1]\\ \textnormal{monotone}\end{subarray}}R_{\mathrm{bd}}(h\circ f;\tau)\;\leq\;2\,\Delta_{\operatorname{Cutoff}}(f). (B.1)

This guarantee implies that if ΔCutoff​(f)\Delta_{\operatorname{Cutoff}}(f) is small, the decision-maker, thresholding f⁡(X)f(X) to make a binary decision, gains little by applying any monotonic recalibration to f⁡(X)f(X). Similarly, they showed that in the binary case, CutOff calibration error can be used to bound distance from calibration. As such, Propositions 3.1 and 3.2 extend the results of Rossellini et al. (2025) to the multiclass setting.

B.2 Bounding Binned Estimators using Utility Calibration

To illustrate the relationship between binned estimations of calibration error and utility calibration, let pX≔f​(X)γ⁡(f⁡(X))p_{X}\coloneqq f(X)_{\gamma(f(X))} and correctness indicator YX≔𝟙{Y=eγ⁡(f⁡(X))}Y_{X}\coloneqq\mathbbm{1}\{Y=e_{\gamma(f(X))}\}, definitions for mm bins (Bj)j∈[m](B_{j})_{j\in[m]} are:

TCEbin​(f)\displaystyle\mathrm{TCE}^{\mathrm{bin}}(f) =∑j=1m|𝔼[(pX−YX)𝟙{pX∈Bj}]|,\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\left|\mathbb{E}\left[\left(p_{X}-Y_{X}\right)\mathbbm{1}\{p_{X}\in B_{j}\}\right]\right|,
UC⁡(f,𝒰TCE)\displaystyle\mathrm{UC}(f,{\cal U}_{\mathrm{TCE}}) =supI∈𝕀⁡[0,1]|𝔼[(YX−pX)𝟙{pX∈I}]|.\displaystyle=\sup_{I\in\mathbb{I}\left[0,1\right]}\left|\mathbb{E}\left[\left(Y_{X}-p_{X}\right)\mathbbm{1}\{p_{X}\in I\}\right]\right|.

Each binned term |𝔼[(pX−YX)𝟙{pX∈Bj}]|≤UC(f,𝒰TCE)\left|\expec\left[(p_{X}-Y_{X})\mathbbm{1}\{p_{X}\in B_{j}\}\right]\right|\leq\mathrm{UC}(f,{\cal U}_{\mathrm{TCE}}) (by setting I=BjI=B_{j}), thus TCEbin​(f)≤m​UC​(f,𝒰TCE)\mathrm{TCE}^{\mathrm{bin}}(f)\leq m\mathrm{UC}(f,{\cal U}_{\mathrm{TCE}}). Conversely, small binned errors do not imply small utility calibration, as binned errors can cancel within bins, while utility calibration is the supremum over intervals.

For instance, let pXp_{X} be 0.450.45 or 0.550.55 (each with probability 0.50.5), with 𝔼[YX|pX=0.45]=0.05\expec[Y_{X}|p_{X}=0.45]=0.05 and 𝔼[YX|pX=0.55]=0.95\expec[Y_{X}|p_{X}=0.55]=0.95. If TCEbin​(f)\mathrm{TCE}^{\mathrm{bin}}(f) uses bins B1=[0,1/3),B2=[1/3,2/3),B3=[2/3,1]B_{1}=[0,1/3),B_{2}=[1/3,2/3),B_{3}=[2/3,1], the expected error is 00. Thus, TCEbin​(f)=0\mathrm{TCE}^{\mathrm{bin}}(f)=0.

However, the inverse is not true. For example, for UC⁡(f,𝒰TCE)\mathrm{UC}(f,{\cal U}_{\mathrm{TCE}}), consider the interval I1=[0.45,0.46]I_{1}=[0.45,0.46]. The term |𝔼[(YX−pX)𝟙{pX∈I1}]|\left|\expec\left[(Y_{X}-p_{X})\mathbbm{1}\{p_{X}\in I_{1}\}\right]\right| becomes |P⁡(pX=0.45)​(𝔼[YX|pX=0.45]−0.45)|=0.2\left|P(p_{X}=0.45)(\expec[Y_{X}|p_{X}=0.45]-0.45)\right|=0.2. Since UC⁡(f,𝒰TCE)\mathrm{UC}(f,{\cal U}_{\mathrm{TCE}}) is the supremum over such intervals, UC⁡(f,𝒰TCE)≥0.2\mathrm{UC}(f,{\cal U}_{\mathrm{TCE}})\geq 0.2. The binned estimator indicates perfect calibration, while UC⁡(f,𝒰TCE)\mathrm{UC}(f,{\cal U}_{\mathrm{TCE}}) does not.

B.3 Hardness of Proactive Measurability

Proactive measurability for a utility class 𝒰{\cal U}, as defined in Definition 4.1, necessitates an algorithm to efficiently find u^∈𝒰\hat{u}\in{\cal U}, whose utility calibration error UC⁡(f,u^)\mathrm{UC}(f,\hat{u}) approximates supu∈𝒰UC⁡(f,u)\sup_{u\in{\cal U}}\mathrm{UC}(f,u). This is equivalent to efficiently finding an approximate worst-case function from the witness class 𝒲(𝒰)=⋃u∈𝒰{X↦ξu→(X)𝟙{vu(X)∈I}∣I∈𝕀[−1,1],ξ∈{−1,1}}\mathcal{W}\left({\cal U}\right)=\bigcup_{u\in{\cal U}}\{X\mapsto\xi\vec{u}(X)\mathbbm{1}\left\{v_{u}(X)\in I\right\}\mid I\in\mathbb{I}\left[-1,1\right],\xi\in\{-1,1\}\}, given that the worst-case interval for a fixed uu is efficiently findable (Lemma 3.3). The work of Gopalan et al. (2024) establishes computational hardness for “auditing with a witness" for related, expressive classes of witness functions.

Definition B.1 (Auditing with a witness (Gopalan et al., 2024)).

An (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) auditor for a witness class 𝒲target\mathcal{W}_{\text{target}} is an algorithm that, when given access to a distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D} where CE𝒲target​(𝒟)>α\mathrm{CE}_{\mathcal{W}_{\text{target}}}(\mathcal{D})>\alpha, returns any function w′:ΔC−1→[−1,1]Cw^{\prime}:\Delta^{C-1}\to[-1,1]^{C} such that 𝔼(𝒳,𝒴)∼𝒟[⟨Y−f⁡(X),w′​(f⁡(X))⟩]≥β.\expec_{(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y})\sim\mathcal{D}}[\left\langle Y-f(X),w^{\prime}(f(X))\right\rangle]\geq\beta.

First, auditing with a witness is an easier task than proactive measurability, as it allows returning any function w′w^{\prime}, not necessarily from the original witness class. Thus, if auditing is hard for a class 𝒲target\mathcal{W}_{\text{target}}, and if our class 𝒲⁡(𝒰)\mathcal{W}({\cal U}) is at least as expressive as 𝒲target\mathcal{W}_{\text{target}}, then proactive measurability for 𝒰{\cal U} is also computationally hard.

Gopalan et al. (2024) demonstrate hardness for two key notions.

  1. 1.

    First, for decision calibration, their witness class 𝒲dec\mathcal{W}_{\text{dec}} involves partitioning ΔC−1\Delta^{C-1} using hyperplanes, i.e. 𝒲dec≔{x→g′𝟙{aTx≥b}+g𝟙{aTx<b}|g′,g,a∈ℝC,b∈ℝ, s.t. ‖g′‖2,‖g‖2≤1}\mathcal{W}_{\text{dec}}\coloneqq\left\{x\rightarrow g^{\prime}\mathbbm{1}\left\{a^{T}x\geq b\right\}+g\mathbbm{1}\left\{a^{T}x<b\right\}|g^{\prime},g,a\in\mathbb{R}^{C},b\in\mathbb{R},\text{ s.t. }\left\lVert g^{\prime}\right\rVert_{2},\left\lVert g\right\rVert_{2}\leq 1\right\}. Auditing for 𝒲dec\mathcal{W}_{\text{dec}} is shown to be computationally hard under standard assumptions (Gopalan et al. (2024, Thm. 5.1)), i.e. cannot be performed in polynomial time for non-trivial α\alpha under standard computational complexity assumptions. Up to a scaling, this is a slightly more general class than 𝒰lin{\cal U}_{\mathrm{lin}}.

  2. 2.

    Second, Gopalan et al. (2024) introduced projected smooth calibration, which is very similar to our notion of utility calibration for 𝒰lin{\cal U}_{\mathrm{lin}}, but replaced the hard interval indicator with Lipschitz functions. Again, auditing for this notion was also proven computationally hard, in the sense that no auditing algorithm can be polynomial in 1/α{1}/{\alpha} (Gopalan et al., 2024, Thm. 8.1).

B.4 Interactive Measurability

In this section, we establish conditions under which the utility calibration error UC⁡(f,𝒰)\mathrm{UC}(f,{\cal U}) is interactively measurable, completing Section 4. This involves bounding the sample complexity required for the empirical estimates UC^​(f,u,S)\widehat{\mathrm{UC}}(f,u;S) to uniformly converge to their true values UC⁡(f,u)\mathrm{UC}(f,u) over all u∈𝒰u\in{\cal U}. Throughout this section, we assume that 𝔼^n\hat{\expec}_{n} denotes the empirical expectation over nn i.i.d. samples.

First, we start by bounding the Rademacher complexity of the class of functions

𝒢𝒰≔{(X,Y)↦⟨Y−f(X),u→(X)𝟙{vu(X)∈I}⟩|u∈𝒰,I∈𝕀[−1,1]}\mathcal{G}_{{\cal U}}\coloneqq\Big\{(X,Y)\mapsto\left\langle Y-f(X),\vec{u}(X)\mathbbm{1}\left\{v_{u}(X)\in I\right\}\right\rangle\;\Big|\;u\in{\cal U},\ I\in\mathbb{I}\left[-1,1\right]\Big\} (B.2)

with respect to its coordinate-wise components 𝒫1,…,𝒫C\mathcal{P}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{P}_{C}, where

𝒫j(𝒰)≔{X↦u(f(X),ej)𝟙{vu(X)∈I}|u∈𝒰,I∈𝕀[−1,1]}.\mathcal{P}_{j}({\cal U})\coloneqq\left\{X\mapsto u(f(X),e_{j})\mathbbm{1}\left\{v_{u}(X)\in I\right\}\;\middle|\;u\in{\cal U},I\in\mathbb{I}\left[-1,1\right]\right\}. (B.3)

This generic bound may be transformed into a sample complexity bound for interactive measurability by Corollary B.5. As an example, we apply it to the class of linear utility functions 𝒰lin{\cal U}_{\mathrm{lin}}. Nonetheless, in Section B.4.1, we derive tighter bounds for 𝒰lin{\cal U}_{\mathrm{lin}} and 𝒰rank{\cal U}_{\mathrm{rank}} by directly bounding their pseudo-dimension. Before proceeding, we first recall standard definitions and results.

Definition B.2.

(Bartlett and Mendelson, 2002, Rademacher Complexity) Let ℱ{\cal F} be a class of real-valued functions h:𝒵→ℝh:\mathcal{Z}\to\mathbb{R}. Given nn samples SZ=(Z1,…,Zn)S_{Z}=(Z_{1},\dots,Z_{n}) where Zi∼DZZ_{i}\sim D_{Z}, the empirical Rademacher complexity of ℱ{\cal F} given SZS_{Z} is

ℜ^n​(ℱ|SZ)=𝔼𝝈​[suph∈ℱ1n​∑i=1nσi​h​(Zi)],\hat{\mathfrak{R}}_{n}({\cal F}|S_{Z})=\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\sigma}}\left[\sup_{h\in{\cal F}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{i}h(Z_{i})\right],

where σi\sigma_{i} are i.i.d. Rademacher random variables. In addition, the expected Rademacher complexity is defined as

ℜn​(ℱ)=𝔼SZ​[ℜ^n​(ℱ|SZ)].\mathfrak{R}_{n}({\cal F})=\mathbb{E}_{S_{Z}}[\hat{\mathfrak{R}}_{n}({\cal F}|S_{Z})].
Definition B.3.

(Vapnik and Chervonenkis, 1971, VC dimension) Let ℋ\mathcal{H} be a class of binary-valued functions on a domain 𝒵\mathcal{Z}. We say that ℋ\mathcal{H} shatters a set {z1,…,zm}⊆𝒵\{z_{1},\ldots,z_{m}\}\subseteq\mathcal{Z} if for every labeling b∈{0,1}mb\in\{0,1\}^{m} there exists h∈ℋh\in\mathcal{H} such that h⁡(zi)=bih(z_{i})=b_{i} for all ii. The VC dimension VC⁡(ℋ)\VC(\mathcal{H}) is the largest mm for which some set of size mm is shattered (or ∞\infty if no such largest mm exists).

Finally, we list a common result combining Massart’s lemma, which bounds the Rademacher complexity using the growth function (Mohri et al., 2018, Theorem 3.7) and Sauer’s lemma, which bounds the growth function (Mohri et al., 2018, Theorem 3.17).

Result 1.

Consider a boolean class of functions ℬ{\cal B} such that d=V​C​(ℬ)d=VC({\cal B}). Let d>nd>n, then it holds that

ℜn​(ℬ)≤2​d​log⁡(e​n/d)n.\mathfrak{R}_{n}({\cal B})\leq\sqrt{\frac{2d\log(en/d)}{n}}.
Theorem B.4 (Rademacher Complexity Bound for 𝒢𝒰\mathcal{G}_{{\cal U}}).

For a utility class 𝒰{\cal U}, the Rademacher complexity of 𝒢𝒰\mathcal{G}_{{\cal U}} is bounded as:

ℜn​(𝒢𝒰)≤2​∑j=1Cℜn​(𝒫j​(𝒰)).\mathfrak{R}_{n}(\mathcal{G}_{{\cal U}})\leq 2\sum_{j=1}^{C}\mathfrak{R}_{n}(\mathcal{P}_{j}({\cal U})).
Proof.

The class 𝒢𝒰\mathcal{G}_{{\cal U}} consists of functions gu,I(X,Y)=⟨Y−f(X),u→(X)𝟙{vu(X)∈I}⟩g_{u,I}(X,Y)=\left\langle Y-f(X),\vec{u}(X)\mathbbm{1}\left\{v_{u}(X)\in I\right\}\right\rangle. We consider the empirical Rademacher complexity ℜ^n​(𝒢𝒰|SX​Y)\hat{\mathfrak{R}}_{n}(\mathcal{G}_{{\cal U}}|S_{XY}) for nn samples SX​Y={(Xk,Yk)}k=1nS_{XY}=\{(X_{k},Y_{k})\}_{k=1}^{n}, which is by definition:

ℜ^n(𝒢𝒰|SX​Y)=𝔼𝝈′[supu∈𝒰I∈𝕀⁡[−1,1]1n∑k=1nσk′⟨Yk−f(Xk),u→(f(Xk))𝟙{vu(Xk)∈I}⟩],\hat{\mathfrak{R}}_{n}(\mathcal{G}_{{\cal U}}|S_{XY})=\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\sigma}^{\prime}}\left[\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}u\in{\cal U}\\ I\in\mathbb{I}\left[-1,1\right]\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n}\sigma^{\prime}_{k}\left\langle Y_{k}-f(X_{k}),\vec{u}(f(X_{k}))\mathbbm{1}\left\{v_{u}(X_{k})\in I\right\}\right\rangle\right],

where σk′\sigma^{\prime}_{k} are i.i.d. scalar Rademacher random variables. For each k∈[n]k\in[n], let Wk=Yk−f⁡(Xk)W_{k}=Y_{k}-f(X_{k}). The function ϕWk:ℝC→ℝ\phi_{W_{k}}:\mathbb{R}^{C}\to\mathbb{R} defined by ϕWk​(z)=⟨Wk,z⟩\phi_{W_{k}}(z)=\left\langle W_{k},z\right\rangle is LL-Lipschitz and ϕWk​(𝟎)=0\phi_{W_{k}}(\mathbf{0})=0. 𝒲→𝒰≔{X↦u→(X)𝟙{vu(X)∈I}|u∈𝒰,I∈𝕀[−1,1]}.\displaystyle\vec{\mathcal{W}}_{{\cal U}}\coloneqq\Big\{X\mapsto\vec{u}(X)\mathbbm{1}\left\{v_{u}(X)\in I\right\}\;\Big|\;u\in{\cal U},\ I\in\mathbb{I}\left[-1,1\right]\Big\}. (B.4)

(B.5)

where 𝝈k∈{−1,1}C\bm{\sigma}_{k}\in\{-1,1\}^{C} are vectors whose components σk​j\sigma_{kj} are i.i.d. Rademacher random variables. Substituting L=2L=\sqrt{2}:

≤𝔼𝝈[∑j=1Csupu∈𝒰I∈𝕀⁡[−1,1]1n∑k=1nσk​ju(f(Xk),ej)𝟙{vu(Xk)∈I}](subadditivity of sup)\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\sigma}}\left[\sum_{j=1}^{C}\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}u\in{\cal U}\\ I\in\mathbb{I}\left[-1,1\right]\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n}\sigma_{kj}u(f(X_{k}),e_{j})\mathbbm{1}\left\{v_{u}(X_{k})\in I\right\}\right]\quad(\text{subadditivity of sup})
