Corollary B.5 (Interactive Measurability from Rademacher Bound).

Let 𝒰{\cal U} be a class of utility functions and 𝒢𝒰\mathcal{G}_{{\cal U}} be the function class defined in eq. B.2. With probability at least 1−δ1-\delta over the draw of S∼DnS\sim D^{n}:

supu∈𝒰|UC^​(f,u,S)−UC⁡(f,u)|≤2​ℜn​(𝒢𝒰)+4​log⁡(2/δ)2​n.\sup_{u\in{\cal U}}|\widehat{\mathrm{UC}}(f,u;S)-\mathrm{UC}(f,u)|\leq 2\mathfrak{R}_{n}(\mathcal{G}_{{\cal U}})+4\sqrt{\frac{\log(2/\delta)}{2n}}.

Combined with Theorem B.4, this implies:

supu∈𝒰|UC^​(f,u,S)−UC⁡(f,u)|≤4​∑j=1Cℜn​(𝒫j​(𝒰))+4​log⁡(2/δ)2​n.\sup_{u\in{\cal U}}|\widehat{\mathrm{UC}}(f,u;S)-\mathrm{UC}(f,u)|\leq 4\sum_{j=1}^{C}\mathfrak{R}_{n}(\mathcal{P}_{j}({\cal U}))+4\sqrt{\frac{\log(2/\delta)}{2n}}.
Proof.

For u∈𝒰u\in{\cal U} and I∈𝕀⁡[−1,1]I\in\mathbb{I}\left[-1,1\right], define gu,I(X,Y)≔⟨Y−f(X),u→(X)𝟙{vu(X)∈I}⟩g_{u,I}(X,Y)\coloneqq\left\langle Y-f(X),\vec{u}(X)\mathbbm{1}\left\{v_{u}(X)\in I\right\}\right\rangle. With UC^​(f,u,S)\widehat{\mathrm{UC}}(f,u;S) defined in Lemma 3.3, it holds by definition that

supu∈𝒰|UC^​(f,u,S)−UC⁡(f,u)|\displaystyle\sup_{u\in{\cal U}}|\widehat{\mathrm{UC}}(f,u;S)-\mathrm{UC}(f,u)| =supu∈𝒰|supI∈𝕀⁡[−1,1]|𝔼^n​[gu,I​(X,Y)]|−supI∈𝕀⁡[−1,1]|𝔼⁡[gu,I​(X,Y)]||\displaystyle=\sup_{u\in{\cal U}}\left|\sup_{I\in\mathbb{I}\left[-1,1\right]}|\hat{\mathbb{E}}_{n}[g_{u,I}(X,Y)]|-\sup_{I\in\mathbb{I}\left[-1,1\right]}|\mathbb{E}[g_{u,I}(X,Y)]|\right|
≤supu∈𝒰supI∈𝕀⁡[−1,1]||𝔼^n​[gu,I​(X,Y)]|−|𝔼⁡[gu,I​(X,Y)]||\displaystyle\leq\sup_{u\in{\cal U}}\sup_{I\in\mathbb{I}\left[-1,1\right]}\left||\hat{\mathbb{E}}_{n}[g_{u,I}(X,Y)]|-|\mathbb{E}[g_{u,I}(X,Y)]|\right|
≤supu∈𝒰supI∈𝕀⁡[−1,1]|𝔼^n​[gu,I​(X,Y)]−𝔼⁡[gu,I​(X,Y)]|\displaystyle\leq\sup_{u\in{\cal U}}\sup_{I\in\mathbb{I}\left[-1,1\right]}\left|\hat{\mathbb{E}}_{n}[g_{u,I}(X,Y)]-\mathbb{E}[g_{u,I}(X,Y)]\right|
=supg∈𝒢𝒰|𝔼^n​[g⁡(X,Y)]−𝔼⁡[g⁡(X,Y)]|.\displaystyle=\sup_{g\in\mathcal{G}_{{\cal U}}}\left|\hat{\mathbb{E}}_{n}[g(X,Y)]-\mathbb{E}[g(X,Y)]\right|.

The first inequality is by supxf⁡(x)−supxg⁡(x)≤supx|(f−g)​(x)|\sup_{x}f(x)-\sup_{x}g(x)\leq\sup_{x}|(f-g)(x)|. Then using (Mohri et al., 2018, Theorem 3.3) (standard symmetrization argument using Rademacher complexity and application of McDiarmid inequality), with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, it holds that

supg∈𝒢𝒰|𝔼^n​[g⁡(X,Y)]−𝔼⁡[g⁡(X,Y)]|≤ 2​ℜn​(𝒢𝒰)+4​log⁡(2/δ)2​n.\displaystyle\sup_{g\in\mathcal{G}_{{\cal U}}}\Big|\hat{\mathbb{E}}_{n}[g(X,Y)]-\mathbb{E}[g(X,Y)]\Big|\;\leq\;2\,\mathfrak{R}_{n}(\mathcal{G}_{{\cal U}})+4\sqrt{\tfrac{\log(2/\delta)}{2n}}\ .

The corollary follows by substituting the bound for ℜn​(𝒢𝒰)\mathfrak{R}_{n}(\mathcal{G}_{{\cal U}}) from Theorem B.4 into the equation above. ∎

We now apply the statements established above to the case of linear utilities (Example 3.5).

Corollary B.6 (Interactive Measurability of 𝒰lin{\cal U}_{\mathrm{lin}}).

The utility calibration error is interactively measurable for the class of linear utilities 𝒰lin{\cal U}_{\mathrm{lin}} (Example 3.5). The sample complexity is N=O⁡(C3​log⁡(n/C)+log⁡(1/δ)ε2)N=O\left(\frac{C^{3}\log(n/C)+\log(1/\delta)}{\varepsilon^{2}}\right).

Proof.

For ua∈𝒰linu_{a}\in{\cal U}_{\mathrm{lin}}, we have, by definition, ua​(f⁡(X),ej)=aju_{a}(f(X),e_{j})=a_{j} (see Example 3.5), where a∈[−1,1]Ca\in[-1,1]^{C}. The predicted utility is vua​(X)=⟨f⁡(X),a⟩v_{u_{a}}(X)=\left\langle f(X),a\right\rangle. The component classes 𝒫j​(𝒰lin)\mathcal{P}_{j}({\cal U}_{\mathrm{lin}}) are:

𝒫j(𝒰lin)={X↦aj𝟙{⟨f(X),a⟩∈I}|a∈[−1,1]C,I∈𝕀[−1,1]}.\displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{j}({\cal U}_{\mathrm{lin}})=\Big\{X\mapsto a_{j}\mathbbm{1}\{\left\langle f(X),a\right\rangle\in I\}\;\Big|\;a\in[-1,1]^{C},\ I\in\mathbb{I}\left[-1,1\right]\Big\}.

Each function in 𝒫j​(𝒰lin)\mathcal{P}_{j}({\cal U}_{\mathrm{lin}}) is a product of aja_{j} and an indicator function 𝟙{⟨f(X),a⟩∈I}\mathbbm{1}\{\left\langle f(X),a\right\rangle\in I\}. First, we consider the class of functions ℋa,I={X↦𝟙{⟨f(X),a⟩∈I}|a∈[−1,1]C,I∈𝕀[−1,1]}\mathcal{H}_{a,I}=\{X\mapsto\mathbbm{1}\{\left\langle f(X),a\right\rangle\in I\}|a\in[-1,1]^{C},I\in\mathbb{I}\left[-1,1\right]\}. ℋa,I{\cal H}_{a,I} is a subclass of the indicator functions of polytopes with two supporting hyperplanes. Thus, VC⁡(ℋa,I)=O⁡(C)\mathrm{VC}\left({\cal H}_{a,I}\right)=O\left(C\right) (Kupavskii, 2020, Theorem 1) and ℜn​(ℋa,I)=O⁡(C​log⁡(n/C)n)\mathfrak{R}_{n}\left({\cal H}_{a,I}\right)=O\left(\sqrt{\frac{C\log(n/C)}{n}}\right). We now proceed to bound ℜn​(𝒫j​(𝒰lin))\mathfrak{R}_{n}\left(\mathcal{P}_{j}\left({\cal U}_{\mathrm{lin}}\right)\right). Let SX={X1,…,Xn}S_{X}=\{X_{1},\dots,X_{n}\} be nn i.i.d. samples. The empirical Rademacher complexity of 𝒫j​(𝒰lin)\mathcal{P}_{j}({\cal U}_{\mathrm{lin}}) is:

ℜ^n​(𝒫j​(𝒰lin)|SX)\displaystyle\hat{\mathfrak{R}}_{n}(\mathcal{P}_{j}({\cal U}_{\mathrm{lin}})|S_{X}) =𝔼𝝈[supa∈[−1,1]CI∈𝕀⁡[−1,1]1n∑k=1nσkaj𝟙{⟨f(Xk),a⟩∈I}]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\sigma}}\left[\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}a\in[-1,1]^{C}\\ I\in\mathbb{I}\left[-1,1\right]\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n}\sigma_{k}a_{j}\mathbbm{1}\{\left\langle f(X_{k}),a\right\rangle\in I\}\right]
≤𝔼𝝈[supa∈[−1,1]CI∈𝕀⁡[−1,1]|aj||1n∑k=1nσk𝟙{⟨f(Xk),a⟩∈I}|]\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\sigma}}\left[\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}a\in[-1,1]^{C}\\ I\in\mathbb{I}\left[-1,1\right]\end{subarray}}|a_{j}|\left|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n}\sigma_{k}\mathbbm{1}\{\left\langle f(X_{k}),a\right\rangle\in I\}\right|\right]
≤𝔼𝝈[supa∈[−1,1]CI∈𝕀⁡[−1,1]|1n∑k=1nσk𝟙{⟨f(Xk),a⟩∈I}|](since |aj|≤1)\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\sigma}}\left[\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}a\in[-1,1]^{C}\\ I\in\mathbb{I}\left[-1,1\right]\end{subarray}}\left|\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n}\sigma_{k}\mathbbm{1}\{\left\langle f(X_{k}),a\right\rangle\in I\}\right|\right]\quad(\text{since }|a_{j}|\leq 1)
=𝔼𝝈​[suph∈ℋa,Iξ∈{−1,1}1n​∑k=1nξ​σk​h​(Xk)].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\sigma}}\left[\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}h\in\mathcal{H}_{a,I}\\ \xi\in\left\{-1,1\right\}\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n}\xi\sigma_{k}h(X_{k})\right].
≤𝔼𝝈[suph∈ℋa,I1n∑k=1nσkh(Xk)]+𝔼𝝈[suph∈ℋa,I1n∑k=1n−σkh(Xk)]\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\sigma}}\left[\sup_{h\in\mathcal{H}_{a,I}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n}\sigma_{k}h(X_{k})\right]+\mathbb{E}_{\bm{\sigma}}\left[\sup_{h\in\mathcal{H}_{a,I}}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n}-\sigma_{k}h(X_{k})\right]
≤2​ℜ^n​(ℋa,I|SX).\displaystyle\leq 2\hat{\mathfrak{R}}_{n}\left({\cal H}_{a,I}|S_{X}\right).

Thus, taking expectations over SXS_{X}:

ℜn​(𝒫j​(𝒰lin))≤2​ℜn​(ℋa,I)=O⁡(C​log⁡(n/C)n).\mathfrak{R}_{n}(\mathcal{P}_{j}({\cal U}_{\mathrm{lin}}))\leq 2\mathfrak{R}_{n}(\mathcal{H}_{a,I})=O\left(\sqrt{\frac{C\log(n/C)}{n}}\right).

Using Corollary B.5, the uniform error bound is:

supu∈𝒰lin|UC^​(f,u,S)−UC⁡(f,u)|\displaystyle\sup_{u\in{\cal U}_{\mathrm{lin}}}|\widehat{\mathrm{UC}}(f,u;S)-\mathrm{UC}(f,u)| ≤4​∑j=1Cℜn​(𝒫j​(𝒰lin))+4​log⁡(2/δ)2​n\displaystyle\leq 4\sum_{j=1}^{C}\mathfrak{R}_{n}(\mathcal{P}_{j}({\cal U}_{\mathrm{lin}}))+4\sqrt{\frac{\log(2/\delta)}{2n}}
=O⁡(C3​log⁡(n/C)n+log⁡(1/δ)n).\displaystyle=O\left(\sqrt{\frac{C^{3}\log(n/C)}{n}+\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{n}}\right).

∎

B.4.1 Sharper interactive measurability for 𝒰lin{\cal U}_{\mathrm{lin}} and 𝒰rank{\cal U}_{\mathrm{rank}}

The generic Rademacher approach of Theorems B.4 and B.5 applies broadly. For linear utilities (Example 3.5) and rank-based utilities (Example 3.6), we obtain sharper bounds by analyzing the pseudo-dimension of the underlying real-valued classes, yielding an O⁡(C​log⁡C)O(C\log C) upper bound with a log-matching Ω⁡(C)\Omega(C) lower bound. We first recall the definition of pseudo-dimension and some standard results.

Definition B.7.

(Anthony and Bartlett, 2009, pseudo-dimension and Subgraph) For a real-valued class ℱ{\cal F} of functions on a domain 𝒵\mathcal{Z}, its subgraph class is

Sub(ℱ)={((z),r)↦𝟙{r≤g(z)}:g∈ℱ}.\Sub({\cal F})\;=\;\big\{\ ((z),r)\mapsto\mathbbm{1}\{r\leq g(z)\}\ :\ g\in{\cal F}\ \big\}.

The pseudo-dimension Pdim⁡(ℱ)\Pdim({\cal F}) is the VC dimension of Sub⁡(ℱ)\Sub({\cal F}).

Result 2.

(Goldberg and Jerrum, 1993, Simplified Version of Theorem 2.2) Let {hθ}θ∈ℝm\{h_{\theta}\}_{\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{m}} be a family of Boolean functions. Suppose that each function hθh_{\theta} is decided by a Boolean formula of constant size whose atomic predicates are linear inequalities in θ\theta. Then, it holds that

VC⁡({hθ:θ∈ℝm})=O⁡(m​log⁡m).\VC\big(\{h_{\theta}:\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{m}\}\big)\ =O\left(m\log m\right).
Result 3.

(Mohri et al., 2018, Theorem 10.6) Let ℱ{\cal F} be a class of functions h:𝒵→ℝh:\mathcal{Z}\to\mathbb{R} with range in [−B,B][-B,B] and Pdim⁡(ℱ)=d\Pdim({\cal F})=d. Then for any δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta over nn i.i.d. samples,

suph∈ℱ|𝔼^n​[h]−𝔼⁡[h]|≤O⁡(B​2​d​log⁡(n/d)+log⁡(1/δ)n).\sup_{h\in{\cal F}}\Big|\widehat{\mathbb{E}}_{n}[h]-\mathbb{E}[h]\Big|\;\leq\;O\left(B\frac{\sqrt{2d\log(n/d)}+\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)}}{\sqrt{n}}\right).

We now give upper and lower bounds on the pseudo-dimension for the linear-utility class and then deduce the resulting sample complexity for interactive measurability. Rank-based utilities will follow via a composition corollary at the end of this section.

Proposition B.8 (pseudo-dimension for 𝒰lin{\cal U}_{\mathrm{lin}}).

Pdim⁡(𝒢lin)=Ω⁡(C)\Pdim(\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{lin}})=\Omega(C) and Pdim⁡(𝒢lin)=O⁡(C​log⁡C)\Pdim(\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{lin}})=O\left(C\log C\right), where 𝒢lin\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{lin}} is the class of functions induced by 𝒰lin{\cal U}_{\mathrm{lin}} as in Equation B.2.

Proof.

For a∈[−1,1]Ca\in[-1,1]^{C} and [s,t]⊆[−1,1][s,t]\subseteq[-1,1], define

ga,s,t(X,Y)=⟨Y−f(X),a⟩{s≤⟨f(X),a⟩≤t},𝒢lin={ga,s,t:a∈[−1,1]C,s≤t∈[−1,1]}.g_{a,s,t}(X,Y)\;=\;\big\langle Y-f(X),\,a\big\rangle\;\mathbbm{1}\!\Big\{\,s\leq\big\langle f(X),a\big\rangle\leq t\,\Big\},\qquad\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{lin}}=\{g_{a,s,t}:a\in[-1,1]^{C},\ s\leq t\in[-1,1]\}.

Let p=f⁡(X)p=f(X) and W=Y−f⁡(X)W=Y-f(X). By the definition of the subgraph class, for any fixed (X,Y)(X,Y) and threshold r∈ℝr\in\mathbb{R},

r≤ga,s,t(X,Y)⇔(s≤⟨p,a⟩≤t∧r≤⟨W,a⟩)∨(¬[s≤⟨p,a⟩≤t]∧r≤0).r\leq g_{a,s,t}(X,Y)\ \iff\ \big(s\leq\langle p,a\rangle\leq t\ \wedge\ r\leq\langle W,a\rangle\big)\ \vee\ \big(\neg[s\leq\langle p,a\rangle\leq t]\ \wedge\ r\leq 0\big).

We introduce the following atomic linear predicates in the parameters (a,s,t)(a,s,t):

A1:⟨p,a⟩−s≥0,A2:t−⟨p,a⟩≥0,\displaystyle A_{1}:\ \langle p,a\rangle-s\geq 0,\qquad A_{2}:\ \;t-\langle p,a\rangle\geq 0,
A3:⟨W,a⟩−r≥0,A4:−r≥0.\displaystyle A_{3}:\ \langle W,a\rangle-r\geq 0,\qquad A_{4}:\ \;-r\geq 0\,.

Note that (A1∧A2)⇔s≤⟨p,a⟩≤t(A_{1}\wedge A_{2})\iff s\leq\langle p,a\rangle\leq t, A3⇔r≤⟨W,a⟩A_{3}\iff r\leq\langle W,a\rangle, and A4⇔r≤0A_{4}\iff r\leq 0. Therefore,

r≤ga,s,t​(X,Y)⇔(A1∧A2∧A3)∨((¬A1∨¬A2)∧A4).r\leq g_{a,s,t}(X,Y)\ \iff\ \big(A_{1}\wedge A_{2}\wedge A_{3}\big)\ \vee\ \big((\neg A_{1}\vee\neg A_{2})\wedge A_{4}\big).

Thus, under the above equivalent, we obtain that Pdim⁡(𝒢lin)=O⁡(C​log⁡(C))\Pdim\left(\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{lin}}\right)=O(C\log(C)), by invoking Result 2 with m=C+2m=C+2.

For the lower bound, take CC points with Y=e1,…,eCY=e_{1},\ldots,e_{C} and p=0p=0; with s=−1,t=1s=-1,t=1, ga,s,t=ajg_{a,s,t}=a_{j} and thus shattering CC points, so Pdim⁡(𝒢lin)≥C\Pdim(\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{lin}})\geq C. ∎

Given the pseudo-dimension bound, we can now directly deduce the sample complexity for interactive measurability.

Corollary B.9 (Sample complexity for 𝒰lin{\cal U}_{\mathrm{lin}}).

Combining Proposition B.8 and Result 3, we obtain that

supu∈𝒰lin|UC^​(f,u,S)−UC⁡(f,u)|≤O⁡(2​C​log⁡(n/C)+log⁡(1/δ)n).\sup_{u\in{\cal U}_{\mathrm{lin}}}\big|\widehat{\mathrm{UC}}(f,u;S)-\mathrm{UC}(f,u)\big|\ \leq\ O\left(\frac{\sqrt{2C\log(n/C)}+\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)}}{\sqrt{n}}\right).

Equivalently, interactive measurability holds with n=O~​((C+log⁡(1/δ))/ε2)n=\tilde{O}\!\big((C+\log(1/\delta))/\varepsilon^{2}\big) for the 𝒰lin{\cal U}_{\mathrm{lin}} class.

Corollary B.10 (Rank utilities via sorting preprocessing).

Let πp\pi_{p} denote the permutation that sorts p=f⁡(X)p=f(X) in descending order and define the fixed ordering map T:(p,Y)↦(p~,Y~)T:(p,Y)\mapsto(\tilde{p},\tilde{Y}) with p~s=pπp​(s)\tilde{p}_{s}=p_{\pi_{p}(s)} and Y~s=Yπp​(s)\tilde{Y}_{s}=Y_{\pi_{p}(s)}. Then, any rank-based utility may be expressed as a linear utility up to a preprocessing with TT. Consequently, Pdim⁡(𝒢𝒰rank)=O⁡(C​log⁡C)\Pdim(\mathcal{G}_{{\cal U}_{\mathrm{rank}}})=O(C\log C) and the sample complexity for interactive measurability for 𝒰rank{\cal U}_{\mathrm{rank}} matches that of 𝒰lin{\cal U}_{\mathrm{lin}}.

Proof.

Let πp\pi_{p} be the permutation that sorts p=f⁡(X)p=f(X) in descending order and define the fixed ordering map T:(p,Y)↦(p~,Y~)T:(p,Y)\mapsto(\tilde{p},\tilde{Y}) with p~s=pπp​(s)\tilde{p}_{s}=p_{\pi_{p}(s)} and Y~s=Yπp​(s)\tilde{Y}_{s}=Y_{\pi_{p}(s)}. For any uθ∈𝒰ranku_{\theta}\in{\cal U}_{\mathrm{rank}}, we have [u→θ​(p)]j=θrank⁡(p,j)[\vec{u}_{\theta}(p)]_{j}=\theta_{\mathrm{rank}(p,j)} and vuθ​(p)=∑s=1Cp~s​θs=⟨p~,θ⟩v_{u_{\theta}}(p)=\sum_{s=1}^{C}\tilde{p}_{s}\,\theta_{s}=\langle\tilde{p},\theta\rangle. Hence, for any interval [s,t]⊆[−1,1][s,t]\subseteq[-1,1],

⟨Y−f(X),u→θ(f(X))⟩ 1{s≤vuθ(f(X))≤t}=⟨Y~−p~,θ⟩ 1{s≤⟨p~,θ⟩≤t},\left\langle Y-f(X),\vec{u}_{\theta}(f(X))\right\rangle\;\mathbbm{1}\{\,s\leq v_{u_{\theta}}(f(X))\leq t\,\}\;=\;\left\langle\tilde{Y}-\tilde{p},\theta\right\rangle\;\mathbbm{1}\{\,s\leq\left\langle\tilde{p},\theta\right\rangle\leq t\,\},

which is exactly the linear-utility template on the transformed sample T⁡(S)T(S). As Proposition B.8 is distribution-independent and TT is a fixed function, we have Pdim⁡(𝒢𝒰rank)=O⁡(C​log⁡C)\Pdim(\mathcal{G}_{{\cal U}_{\mathrm{rank}}})=O(C\log C). Interactive measurability follows from Result 3, similarly to Corollary B.9. ∎

B.5 Quantile Guarantees

The evaluation methodology in Section 5 relies on plotting the empirical CDF F^E,M,n\widehat{F}_{E,M,n}, constructed from MM utility functions and nn data points. F^E,M,n\widehat{F}_{E,M,n} serves as a proxy for the true CDF FEF_{E} of utility calibration errors. Theorem B.11 bounds the distance between the curves, as characterized by the L2L_{2}-distance. While weaker than characterizing the deviation using L∞L_{\infty}-norm, L2L_{2} distance allows a bound without any assumptions on the smoothness of the underlying CDF FEF_{E}. The bound depends on two factors: first, the uniform accuracy εstat\varepsilon_{\text{stat}} with which individual utility calibration errors UC⁡(f,u)\mathrm{UC}(f,u) can be estimated by UC^​(f,u,S)\widehat{\mathrm{UC}}(f,u;S), and second, the number of utility functions MM sampled to construct the F^E,M,n\widehat{F}_{E,M,n}.

Theorem B.11.

Let FE​(e)≔ℙu∼𝒟𝒰(UC⁡(f,u)≤e)F_{E}(e)\coloneqq\prob_{u\sim\mathcal{D}_{{\cal U}}}(\mathrm{UC}(f,u)\leq e) be the true CDF of utility calibration errors, where uu is drawn from a distribution 𝒟𝒰\mathcal{D}_{{\cal U}} over the utility class 𝒰{\cal U}. Let F^E,M,n(e)≔1M∑m=1M𝟙{UC^(f,um;S)≤e}\widehat{F}_{E,M,n}(e)\coloneqq\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\mathbbm{1}\{\widehat{\mathrm{UC}}(f,u_{m};S)\leq e\} be its empirical estimate, based on MM i.i.d. utility functions u1,…,uM∼𝒟𝒰u_{1},\ldots,u_{M}\sim\mathcal{D}_{{\cal U}} and a data sample SS of size n⁡(δS,εstat)n\left(\delta_{S},\varepsilon_{\text{stat}}\right). Assume that, with probability at least 1−δS1-\delta_{S} over the draw of SS,

supu∈𝒰|UC^​(f,u,S)−UC⁡(f,u)|≤εstat.\sup_{u\in{\cal U}}|\widehat{\mathrm{UC}}(f,u;S)-\mathrm{UC}(f,u)|\leq\varepsilon_{\text{stat}}.

Then, with probability at least (1−δS−δM)(1-\delta_{S}-\delta_{M}) over the draw of SS and {um}m=1M\{u_{m}\}_{m=1}^{M}, it holds that

‖FE−F^E,M,n‖L2​([0,2])≤2​εstat+ln⁡(2/δM)M.\|F_{E}-\widehat{F}_{E,M,n}\|_{L^{2}([0,2])}\;\leq\;\sqrt{2\varepsilon_{\text{stat}}}+\sqrt{\frac{\ln(2/\delta_{M})}{M}}.
Proof.

Let E⁡(u)≔UC⁡(f,u)E(u)\coloneqq\mathrm{UC}(f,u) be the true utility calibration error for a utility function u∼𝒟𝒰u\sim\mathcal{D}_{{\cal U}}, and let E^S​(u)≔UC^​(f,u,S)\widehat{E}_{S}(u)\coloneqq\widehat{\mathrm{UC}}(f,u;S) be its empirical estimate based on data sample SS. The CDF of E⁡(u)E(u) is FEF_{E}, and let FE^SF_{\widehat{E}_{S}} be the CDF of E^S​(u)\widehat{E}_{S}(u) when u∼𝒟𝒰u\sim\mathcal{D}_{{\cal U}} and SS is fixed.

We condition on the event (occurring with probability at least 1−δS1-\delta_{S}) that SS is such that |E⁡(u)−E^S​(u)|≤εstat|E(u)-\widehat{E}_{S}(u)|\leq\varepsilon_{\text{stat}} for all u∈𝒰u\in{\cal U}. This implies that for any uu, E⁡(u)−εstat≤E^S​(u)≤E⁡(u)+εstatE(u)-\varepsilon_{\text{stat}}\leq\widehat{E}_{S}(u)\leq E(u)+\varepsilon_{\text{stat}}. Consequently, for any u∈𝒰u\in{\cal U}, as E⁡(u)E(u) and E^​(u)\hat{E}(u) belong to the set [0,2]\left[0,2\right], it holds for any e∈[0,2]e\in[0,2] that

FE​(e−εstat)=ℙ(E⁡(u)≤e−εstat)≤ℙ(E^S​(u)≤e)=FE^S​(e)\displaystyle F_{E}(e-\varepsilon_{\text{stat}})\;=\;\prob(E(u)\leq e-\varepsilon_{\text{stat}})\;\leq\;\prob(\widehat{E}_{S}(u)\leq e)\;=\;F_{\widehat{E}_{S}}(e)
FE^S​(e)=ℙ(E^S​(u)≤e)≤ℙ(E⁡(u)≤e+εstat)=FE​(e+εstat).\displaystyle F_{\widehat{E}_{S}}(e)\;=\;\prob(\widehat{E}_{S}(u)\leq e)\;\leq\;\prob(E(u)\leq e+\varepsilon_{\text{stat}})\;=\;F_{E}(e+\varepsilon_{\text{stat}}).

Thus, FE​(e−εstat)≤FE^S​(e)≤FE​(e+εstat)F_{E}(e-\varepsilon_{\text{stat}})\leq F_{\widehat{E}_{S}}(e)\leq F_{E}(e+\varepsilon_{\text{stat}}). This implies that

|FE^S​(e)−FE​(e)|≤max⁡{FE​(e+εstat)−FE​(e),FE​(e)−FE​(e−εstat)}.|F_{\widehat{E}_{S}}(e)-F_{E}(e)|\;\leq\;\max\{F_{E}(e+\varepsilon_{\text{stat}})-F_{E}(e),F_{E}(e)-F_{E}(e-\varepsilon_{\text{stat}})\}.

Let ΔE​(e)\Delta_{E}(e) denote the right-hand side. The L2L^{2} distance squared between FE^SF_{\widehat{E}_{S}} and FEF_{E} is

≤∫02ΔE​(e)2​𝑑e≤∫02ΔE​(e)​𝑑e,\displaystyle\leq\int_{0}^{2}\Delta_{E}(e)^{2}\mathrm{d}e\;\leq\;\int_{0}^{2}\Delta_{E}(e)\mathrm{d}e,

since 0≤ΔE​(e)≤10\leq\Delta_{E}(e)\leq 1. Further, as max⁡(a,b)≤a+b\max(a,b)\leq a+b for non-negative a,ba,b, it follows that

The first term evaluates to ∫22+εstatFE​(v)​𝑑v−∫0εstatFE​(v)​𝑑v\int_{2}^{2+\varepsilon_{\text{stat}}}F_{E}(v)dv-\int_{0}^{\varepsilon_{\text{stat}}}F_{E}(v)dv. Since FE​(v)=1F_{E}(v)=1 for v≥2v\geq 2 and FE​(v)≥0F_{E}(v)\geq 0, this term is ≤εstat\leq\varepsilon_{\text{stat}}. The second term evaluates to ∫2−εstat2FE​(v)​𝑑v−∫−εstat0FE​(v)​𝑑v\int_{2-\varepsilon_{\text{stat}}}^{2}F_{E}(v)dv-\int_{-\varepsilon_{\text{stat}}}^{0}F_{E}(v)dv. Since FE​(v)=0F_{E}(v)=0 for v<0v<0 (errors are non-negative) and FE​(v)≤1F_{E}(v)\leq 1, this term is ≤εstat\leq\varepsilon_{\text{stat}}. Thus, ∫02ΔE​(e)​𝑑e≤2​εstat\int_{0}^{2}\Delta_{E}(e)de\leq 2\varepsilon_{\text{stat}}, which implies ‖FE^S−FE‖L2​([0,2])≤2​εstat\|F_{\widehat{E}_{S}}-F_{E}\|_{L^{2}([0,2])}\leq\sqrt{2\varepsilon_{\text{stat}}}.

Next, F^E,M,n​(e)\widehat{F}_{E,M,n}(e) is the empirical CDF of MM i.i.d. samples {E^S​(um)}m=1M\{\widehat{E}_{S}(u_{m})\}_{m=1}^{M} drawn according to FE^SF_{\widehat{E}_{S}}. By the Dvoretzky–Kiefer–Wolfowitz (DKW) inequality (Massart, 1990), with probability at least 1−δM1-\delta_{M}:

≤∫02‖F^E,M,n−FE^S‖∞2​𝑑e\displaystyle\leq\int_{0}^{2}\|\widehat{F}_{E,M,n}-F_{\widehat{E}_{S}}\|_{\infty}^{2}\mathrm{d}e
=2​‖F^E,M,n−FE^S‖∞2≤ln⁡(2/δM)M.\displaystyle=2\|\widehat{F}_{E,M,n}-F_{\widehat{E}_{S}}\|_{\infty}^{2}\;\leq\;\frac{\ln(2/\delta_{M})}{M}.

So, ‖FE^S−F^E,M,n‖L2​([0,2])≤ln⁡(2/δM)M\|F_{\widehat{E}_{S}}-\widehat{F}_{E,M,n}\|_{L^{2}([0,2])}\leq\sqrt{\frac{\ln(2/\delta_{M})}{M}}. Finally, by the triangle inequality, combining the two bounds:

Using a union bound, this holds with probability at least (1−δS−δM)(1-\delta_{S}-\delta_{M}). ∎

B.6 Proofs

We now proceed to the proofs of the statements in the main paper.

B.7 Proof of Proposition 3.1

Proof.

At a high-level, the proof is similar to the approach of Rossellini et al. (2025) but some details differ. We start by analyzing the loss function

ℓutil(uY,U^;t0)=(t0−uY)(U^−𝟙{uY≥t0}).\ell_{\mathrm{util}}(u_{Y},\hat{U};t_{0})=(t_{0}-u_{Y})(\hat{U}-\mathbbm{1}\left\{u_{Y}\geq t_{0}\right\}). (B.6)
  • •

    If U^=𝟙{uY≥t0}\hat{U}=\mathbbm{1}\left\{u_{Y}\geq t_{0}\right\}, then ℓutil=0\ell_{\mathrm{util}}=0.

  • •

    If U^=1\hat{U}=1 and uY<t0u_{Y}<t_{0}, the loss is t0−uY>0t_{0}-u_{Y}>0.

  • •

    If U^=0\hat{U}=0 but uY≥t0u_{Y}\geq t_{0} , the loss is uY−t0≥0u_{Y}-t_{0}\geq 0.

The loss, which is only non-zero when a mismatch U^≠𝟙{uY≥t0}\hat{U}\neq\mathbbm{1}\left\{u_{Y}\geq t_{0}\right\} occurs, is |uY−t0||u_{Y}-t_{0}|. This loss function penalizes mismatches between the action taken based on vu​(X)v_{u}(X) and the ideal action based on uYu_{Y}. We now consider any monotone non-decreasing function h:[−1,1]→[−1,1].h:\left[-1,1\right]\rightarrow[-1,1]. The difference in risks between using vu​(X)v_{u}(X) directly and using h​(vu​(X))h(v_{u}(X)) is

Δ​R\displaystyle\Delta R =Rutil​(vu​(X),t0)−Rutil​(h⁡(vu​(X)),t0)\displaystyle=R_{\mathrm{util}}(v_{u}(X);t_{0})-R_{\mathrm{util}}(h(v_{u}(X));t_{0})
=𝔼[(t0−uY)(𝟙{vu(X)≥t0}−𝟙{uY≥t0})]−𝔼[(t0−uY)(𝟙{h(vu(X))≥t0}−𝟙{uY≥t0})]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\Big[(t_{0}-u_{Y})(\mathbbm{1}\left\{v_{u}(X)\geq t_{0}\right\}-\mathbbm{1}\left\{u_{Y}\geq t_{0}\right\})\Big]-\mathbb{E}\Big[(t_{0}-u_{Y})(\mathbbm{1}\left\{h(v_{u}(X))\geq t_{0}\right\}-\mathbbm{1}\left\{u_{Y}\geq t_{0}\right\})\Big]
=𝔼[(t0−uY)(𝟙{vu(X)≥t0}−𝟙{h(vu(X))≥t0})].\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\Big[(t_{0}-u_{Y})(\mathbbm{1}\left\{v_{u}(X)\geq t_{0}\right\}-\mathbbm{1}\left\{h(v_{u}(X))\geq t_{0}\right\})\Big].

Let E1={X∣vu(X)<t0,h(vu(X))≥t0}E_{1}=\{X\mid v_{u}(X)<t_{0},h(v_{u}(X))\geq t_{0}\} and E2={X∣vu(X)≥t0,h(vu(X))<t0}E_{2}=\{X\mid v_{u}(X)\geq t_{0},h(v_{u}(X))<t_{0}\}. The term 𝟙{vu(X)≥t0}−𝟙{h(vu(X))≥t0}\mathbbm{1}\left\{v_{u}(X)\geq t_{0}\right\}-\mathbbm{1}\left\{h(v_{u}(X))\geq t_{0}\right\} equals −1-1 on E1E_{1} and 11 on E2E_{2}, and 00 elsewhere.

Δ​R\displaystyle\Delta R =𝔼[(t0−uY)(−𝟙{X∈E1})+(t0−uY)(𝟙{X∈E2})]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\Big[(t_{0}-u_{Y})(-\mathbbm{1}\left\{X\in E_{1}\right\})+(t_{0}-u_{Y})(\mathbbm{1}\left\{X\in E_{2}\right\})\Big]
=𝔼[(uY−t0)𝟙{X∈E1}]−𝔼[(uY−t0)𝟙{X∈E2}]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\Big[(u_{Y}-t_{0})\mathbbm{1}\left\{X\in E_{1}\right\}\Big]-\mathbb{E}\Big[(u_{Y}-t_{0})\mathbbm{1}\left\{X\in E_{2}\right\}\Big]
=𝔼[(uY−vu(X)+vu(X)−t0)𝟙{X∈E1}]−𝔼[(uY−vu(X)+vu(X)−t0)𝟙{X∈E2}]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\Big[(u_{Y}-v_{u}(X)+v_{u}(X)-t_{0})\mathbbm{1}\left\{X\in E_{1}\right\}\Big]-\mathbb{E}\Big[(u_{Y}-v_{u}(X)+v_{u}(X)-t_{0})\mathbbm{1}\left\{X\in E_{2}\right\}\Big]
=𝔼[(uY−vu(X))𝟙{X∈E1}]⏟A+𝔼[(vu(X)−t0)𝟙{X∈E1}]⏟C\displaystyle=\underbrace{\mathbb{E}\Big[(u_{Y}-v_{u}(X))\mathbbm{1}\left\{X\in E_{1}\right\}\Big]}_{A}+\underbrace{\mathbb{E}\Big[(v_{u}(X)-t_{0})\mathbbm{1}\left\{X\in E_{1}\right\}\Big]}_{C}
−𝔼[(uY−vu(X))𝟙{X∈E2}]⏟B−𝔼[(vu(X)−t0)𝟙{X∈E2}]⏟D.\displaystyle\quad-\underbrace{\mathbb{E}\Big[(u_{Y}-v_{u}(X))\mathbbm{1}\left\{X\in E_{2}\right\}\Big]}_{B}-\underbrace{\mathbb{E}\Big[(v_{u}(X)-t_{0})\mathbbm{1}\left\{X\in E_{2}\right\}\Big]}_{D}.

On E1E_{1}, we have vu​(X)<t0v_{u}(X)<t_{0}, which implies vu​(X)−t0<0v_{u}(X)-t_{0}<0, so C≤0C\leq 0. On E2E_{2}, we have vu​(X)≥t0v_{u}(X)\geq t_{0}, which implies vu​(X)−t0≥0v_{u}(X)-t_{0}\geq 0, so D≥0D\geq 0. Thus, Δ​R=A+C−B−D≤A−B\Delta R=A+C-B-D\leq A-B. A−B=𝔼[(uY−vu(X))𝟙{X∈E1}]+𝔼[(vu(X)−uY)𝟙{X∈E2}]A-B=\mathbb{E}[(u_{Y}-v_{u}(X))\mathbbm{1}\left\{X\in E_{1}\right\}]+\mathbb{E}[(v_{u}(X)-u_{Y})\mathbbm{1}\left\{X\in E_{2}\right\}]. Since hh is monotone non-decreasing, the sets E1E_{1} and E2E_{2} correspond to vu​(X)v_{u}(X) lying within specific intervals (or unions of intervals which can be decomposed). Let I1I_{1} be the set of vu​(X)v_{u}(X) values defining E1E_{1} (e.g., vu​(X)<t0v_{u}(X)<t_{0} and h⁡(vu​(X))≥t0h(v_{u}(X))\geq t_{0}) and I2I_{2} be the set for E2E_{2}. The terms 𝟙{X∈E1}\mathbbm{1}\left\{X\in E_{1}\right\} and 𝟙{X∈E2}\mathbbm{1}\left\{X\in E_{2}\right\} effectively restrict the expectation to regions where vu​(X)v_{u}(X) falls into certain ranges. By the definition of UC⁡(f,u)\mathrm{UC}(f,u), for E∈{E1,E2}E\in\left\{E_{1},E_{2}\right\} 𝔼[(uY−vu(X))𝟙{X∈E}]≤supI∈𝕀⁡[−1,1]|𝔼[(uY−vu(X))𝟙{vu(X)∈I}]|≤UC(f,u)\mathbb{E}[(u_{Y}-v_{u}(X))\mathbbm{1}\left\{X\in E\right\}]\leq\sup_{I\in\mathbb{I}\left[-1,1\right]}\left\lvert\mathbb{E}[(u_{Y}-v_{u}(X))\mathbbm{1}\left\{v_{u}(X)\in I\right\}]\right\rvert\leq\mathrm{UC}(f,u).

Therefore, Δ​R≤A−B≤UC⁡(f,u)+UC⁡(f,u)=2​UC​(f,u)\Delta R\leq A-B\leq\mathrm{UC}(f,u)+\mathrm{UC}(f,u)=2\mathrm{UC}(f,u). Since this holds for any monotone non-decreasing function hh, taking the supremum over monotone functions completes the proof. ∎

B.8 Proof of Proposition 3.2

Proof.

The proof is the same as (Rossellini et al., 2025, Lemma A.2.), we include it for completeness. Assume UC⁡(f,u)>0\mathrm{UC}(f,u)>0. Let UY≔u⁡(f⁡(X),Y)U_{Y}\coloneqq u(f(X),Y) denote the realized utility. Both UYU_{Y} and vu​(X)v_{u}(X) take values in [−1,1][-1,1].

Let W∈(0,2]W\in(0,2] be a chosen bin width. We partition the interval [−1,1][-1,1] into KW=⌈2/W⌉K_{W}=\lceil 2/W\rceil disjoint intervals A1,A2,…,AKWA_{1},A_{2},\ldots,A_{K_{W}}. These intervals are constructed as follows: For j=1,…,KW−1j=1,\ldots,K_{W}-1, let Aj=[−1+(j−1)W,−1+jW)A_{j}=[-1+(j-1)W,-1+jW). For j=KWj=K_{W}, let AKW=[−1+(KW−1)​W,1]A_{K_{W}}=[-1+(K_{W}-1)W,1]. This construction ensures that ⋃j=1KWAj=[−1,1]\bigcup_{j=1}^{K_{W}}A_{j}=[-1,1], and each interval AjA_{j} has length λ⁡(Aj)≤W\lambda(A_{j})\leq W.

Let ψW:[−1,1]→{1,…,KW}\psi_{W}:[-1,1]\to\{1,\ldots,K_{W}\} be the function mapping a value z∈[−1,1]z\in[-1,1] to the index jj of the bin AjA_{j} such that z∈Ajz\in A_{j}. We construct a candidate calibrated predictor gW​(X)≔𝔼⁡[UY∣ψW​(vu​(X))]g_{W}(X)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}[U_{Y}\mid\psi_{W}(v_{u}(X))]. The function gW​(X)g_{W}(X) is perfectly calibrated: 𝔼⁡[UY∣gW​(X)]=𝔼⁡[𝔼⁡[UY∣ψW​(vu​(X))]∣gW​(X)]\mathbb{E}[U_{Y}\mid g_{W}(X)]=\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[U_{Y}\mid\psi_{W}(v_{u}(X))]\mid g_{W}(X)]. Since gW​(X)g_{W}(X) is, by definition, measurable with respect to the sigma-algebra generated by ψW​(vu​(X))\psi_{W}(v_{u}(X)), it follows from the properties of conditional expectation that 𝔼⁡[UY∣gW​(X)]=gW​(X)\mathbb{E}[U_{Y}\mid g_{W}(X)]=g_{W}(X) almost surely.

By the definition of DCU⁡(f,u)\mathrm{DCU}(f,u), which is the infimum of distances 𝔼​|g⁡(X)−vu​(X)|\mathbb{E}|g(X)-v_{u}(X)| over all perfectly calibrated predictors g⁡(X)g(X), it holds that DCU⁡(f,u)≤𝔼​|gW​(X)−vu​(X)|\mathrm{DCU}(f,u)\leq\mathbb{E}|g_{W}(X)-v_{u}(X)|. To analyze the right-hand side, we introduce an intermediate term Vavgbin​(X)≔𝔼⁡[vu​(X)∣ψW​(vu​(X))]V_{\mathrm{avgbin}}(X)\coloneqq\mathbb{E}[v_{u}(X)\mid\psi_{W}(v_{u}(X))]. This represents the average of vu​(X)v_{u}(X) within the bin AψW​(vu​(X))A_{\psi_{W}(v_{u}(X))} where vu​(X)v_{u}(X) falls. Using the triangle inequality: 𝔼​|gW​(X)−vu​(X)|≤𝔼​|gW​(X)−Vavgbin​(X)|+𝔼​|Vavgbin​(X)−vu​(X)|\mathbb{E}|g_{W}(X)-v_{u}(X)|\leq\mathbb{E}|g_{W}(X)-V_{\mathrm{avgbin}}(X)|+\mathbb{E}|V_{\mathrm{avgbin}}(X)-v_{u}(X)|.

To bound the second term, 𝔼​|Vavgbin​(X)−vu​(X)|\mathbb{E}|V_{\mathrm{avgbin}}(X)-v_{u}(X)|: For any realization X=xX=x, vu​(x)v_{u}(x) is a point in some bin AjA_{j}. Vavgbin​(x)V_{\mathrm{avgbin}}(x) is the conditional expectation of vu​(X′)v_{u}(X^{\prime}) given that vu​(X′)v_{u}(X^{\prime}) is in AjA_{j}. As such, Vavgbin​(x)V_{\mathrm{avgbin}}(x) must also lie within the convex hull of AjA_{j}. Thus, |Vavgbin​(x)−vu​(x)|≤W|V_{\mathrm{avgbin}}(x)-v_{u}(x)|\leq W. Taking the expectation over XX, we get 𝔼​|Vavgbin​(X)−vu​(X)|≤W\mathbb{E}|V_{\mathrm{avgbin}}(X)-v_{u}(X)|\leq W.

To bound the first term:

𝔼​|gW​(X)−Vavgbin​(X)|\displaystyle\mathbb{E}|g_{W}(X)-V_{\mathrm{avgbin}}(X)| =𝔼​|𝔼⁡[UY∣ψW​(vu​(X))]−𝔼⁡[vu​(X)∣ψW​(vu​(X))]|\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left|\mathbb{E}[U_{Y}\mid\psi_{W}(v_{u}(X))]-\mathbb{E}[v_{u}(X)\mid\psi_{W}(v_{u}(X))]\right|

Therefore, 𝔼​|gW​(X)−Vavgbin​(X)|≤∑j=1KWUC⁡(f,u)=KW​UC​(f,u)\mathbb{E}|g_{W}(X)-V_{\mathrm{avgbin}}(X)|\leq\sum_{j=1}^{K_{W}}\mathrm{UC}(f,u)=K_{W}\mathrm{UC}(f,u). B.9 Proof of Lemma 3.3

Proof.

Let A⁡(X,Y):=u⁡(f⁡(X),Y)−vu​(X)A(X,Y):=u(f(X),Y)-v_{u}(X) and V:=vu​(X)V:=v_{u}(X). Since u⁡(⋅,⋅),vu​(⋅)∈[−1,1]u(\cdot,\cdot),v_{u}(\cdot)\in[-1,1], we have A⁡(X,Y)∈[−2,2]A(X,Y)\in[-2,2] and V∈[−1,1]V\in[-1,1] almost surely. For any interval I∈𝕀⁡[−1,1]I\in\mathbb{I}\left[-1,1\right], define

ℱint:={hI:(X,Y)↦A(X,Y) 1{V∈I}|I∈𝕀[−1,1]},\displaystyle{\cal F}_{\mathrm{int}}:=\big\{\,h_{I}:(X,Y)\mapsto A(X,Y)\,\mathbbm{1}\left\{V\in I\right\}\ \big|\ I\in\mathbb{I}\left[-1,1\right]\,\big\},
ℱ≤:={ht:(X,Y)↦A(X,Y) 1{V≤t}|t∈[−1,1]}.\displaystyle{\cal F}_{\leq}:=\big\{\,h_{t}:(X,Y)\mapsto A(X,Y)\,\mathbbm{1}\left\{V\leq t\right\}\ \big|\ t\in[-1,1]\,\big\}.

By definition,

UC⁡(f,u)=supI∈𝕀⁡[−1,1]|𝔼⁡[hI]|,UC^​(f,u,S)=supI∈𝕀⁡[−1,1]|𝔼^n​[hI]|,\mathrm{UC}(f,u)\,=\,\sup_{I\in\mathbb{I}\left[-1,1\right]}\big|\mathbb{E}[h_{I}]\big|,\qquad\widehat{\mathrm{UC}}(f,u;S)\,=\,\sup_{I\in\mathbb{I}\left[-1,1\right]}\big|\hat{\mathbb{E}}_{n}[h_{I}]\big|,

Appendix C Additional Experiments

Section C.1 describes datasets, models, and calibration methods. Section C.2 takes a deeper look at the empirical behavior of Algorithm 1. To this end, it demonstrates the empirical behavior of Algorithm 1 on two families of utility functions: aligned and misaligned. Finally, Section C.3 compiles extended tables and eCDF plots across CIFAR10/100, ImageNet, and an additional text classification experiment. In addition, it introduces two additional utility function classes; one inspired by discounted cumulative gain (DCG) (Järvelin and Kekäläinen, 2002) and the other inspired by semantic-based classification loss (Deng et al., 2012).

C.1 Experimental Details

Experimental Setup: Our experiments were performed using standard image classification benchmarks: CIFAR10, CIFAR100 (Krizhevsky et al., 2009, MIT License), ImageNet-1K (Deng et al., 2009, provided for non-commercial use), and the test split of Yahoo Answers Topics (Zhang et al., 2015, non-commercial use). We used publicly available pretrained models. For each model–dataset combination, the validation data was divided into a calibration set (70%70\%) for training post-hoc methods and a test set (30%30\%) for evaluation. We repeated the experiments across 1010 different calibration/test splits and reported the average results. For CIFAR10/100 datasets, we used the model checkpoints available in Chen (2020). For ImageNet-1K, we used timm checkpoints (Wightman, ). For text classification, we used the publicly available model https://huggingface.co/Koushim/distilbert-yahoo-answers-topic-classifier, provided under the Apache 2.0 license. All post-hoc methods were trained on the designated calibration set and subsequently evaluated on the test set. All experiments (including hyperparameter tuning) took approximately 120 hours on an A100 80GB NVIDIA GPU.

Calibration Methods and Evaluation: We benchmarked several well-known post-hoc calibration techniques. These include Temperature Scaling (Temp. S.) (Platt et al., 1999; Guo et al., 2017), Vector Scaling (V.S.) (Kull et al., 2017; Guo et al., 2017), Dirichlet recalibration (Kull et al., 2019) with off-diagonal regularization (ODIR), and Isotonic Regression (I.R.) (Zadrozny and Elkan, 2002), applied both globally and in a one-vs-all manner. For these methods, we based our implementation on the publicly available code in (Salvador, 2022). For Dirichlet recalibration, we tuned the regularization parameter over 8080 runs using BayesSearchCV from scikit-optimize (Head et al., 2018) with the goal of minimizing the negative log-likelihood.

Algorithm 1 implementation:

Building on the algorithmic template in Algorithm 1, our implementation iteratively (i) audits to find the worst witness over the chosen utility class using the worst-interval estimator, and (ii) applies a masked update along that witness only for points whose predicted utility falls in the identified interval, followed by projection onto the probability simplex. For the stepsize selection, we also employ a backtracking Armijo line search, using JAXOPT (Blondel et al., 2021), to choose a stepsize that decreases the Brier score. The implementation minimizes the utility calibration against the union class 𝒰=𝒰CWE∪𝒰topK{\cal U}={\cal U}_{\mathrm{CWE}}\cup{\cal U}_{\mathrm{topK}}, as defined in Section 3. In addition, at each step, we sampled 264264 utility functions from 𝒰rank{\cal U}_{\mathrm{rank}} and 𝒰lin{\cal U}_{\mathrm{lin}} to augment the set of utility functions. Hyperparameter tuning was performed using scikit-optimize (Head et al., 2018) over the stepsize, the number of steps, and whether to sample additional utility functions from 𝒰rank{\cal U}_{\mathrm{rank}} and 𝒰lin{\cal U}_{\mathrm{lin}}. For hyperparameter tuning, we performed 2020 runs.

Evaluation. Model performance and calibration were assessed using a suite of metrics. Standard evaluations included Accuracy and Brier score. For binned binarized approaches, we compute TCEbin\mathrm{TCE}^{\mathrm{bin}} (2.1) and CWEbin\mathrm{CWE}^{\mathrm{bin}} (2.2), using 1515 equal-weight bins (each bin has the same number of datapoints). Furthermore, we evaluated our proposed binning-free utility calibration metrics for specific utility classes: 𝒰TCE{\cal U}_{\mathrm{TCE}}, 𝒰CWE{\cal U}_{\mathrm{CWE}}, and 𝒰topK{\cal U}_{\mathrm{topK}}. In addition, we computed other utility calibration metrics for specific utility classes described in Section C.3.

C.2 Algorithm 1 for Aligned and Misaligned Utility Classes

To better understand the dynamics of calibrating against different utility structures, this set of experiments focuses on the convergence speed (and final performance) of Algorithm 1 when faced with “aligned” versus “misaligned” non-linear utility classes.

Utility model. Let R∈[0,1]C×CR\in[0,1]^{C\times C} be a user-defined gain matrix with Ri​i=1R_{ii}=1, where Ri​jR_{ij} is the gain for predicting class jj when the true class is ii. For a prediction p=f⁡(X)p=f(X), a rational agent may choose

j⋆​(p)=argmaxj∈[C]​∑i=1Cpi​Ri​j.j^{\star}(p)\;=\;\mathrm{argmax}_{j\in[C]}\ \sum_{i=1}^{C}p_{i}\,R_{ij}.

As we consider the utility function

uR​(p,y=ei)=Ri,j⋆​(p).u_{R}(p,\,y=e_{i})\;=\;R_{i,\,j^{\star}(p)}\,.

Consistent with our framework, we use the associated regressor vuR​(X)≔∑i=1Cf​(X)i​Ri,j⋆​(f​(X))v_{u_{R}}(X)\coloneqq\sum_{i=1}^{C}f(X)_{i}\,R_{i,\,j^{\star}(f(X))}.

We investigate two utility classes to simulate two scenarios: one with all users having the same preferences (aligned) and the other with users having distinct preferences (misaligned).

  • •

    Aligned class: models users with a low tolerance for any error. We set Ri​i=1R_{ii}=1 and sample all off-diagonal entries (i≠ji\neq j) i.i.d. from Unif⁡(0,0.1)\mathrm{Unif}(0,0.1).

  • •

    Misaligned class: models a mix of specialists with distinct biases. We partition the labels into disjoint subsets (K1,K2,…)(K_{1},K_{2},\dots). For a user specializing in KmK_{m}, we set Ri​i=1R_{ii}=1, Ri​j=0.2R_{ij}=0.2 for all j∈Kmj\in K_{m} with i≠ji\neq j, and all other off-diagonals to 00. The utility class is a mixture over such specialists.

Evaluation. We illustrate the performance of Algorithm 1 on these classes on CIFAR100 and ImageNet-1K, using ViT and ResNet56 checkpoints. For each utility class, we sampled 512512 utility functions per iteration. For each dataset, we track (i) the trajectory of the utility calibration error across iterations of Algorithm 1 for both aligned and misaligned classes (see Figure 2), and (ii) the distribution of per-example utility calibration errors at selected iterations to visualize distributional shifts across the class (see Figure 3). In summary, we provide three panels for each dataset: the iteration curve and two distributional grids (aligned and misaligned).

Interpretation. Across both datasets and both utility families (aligned and misaligned), the worst-case sampled utility calibration error initially drops and then stabilizes. Nonetheless, utility calibration error distributions shift toward smaller values over iterations. Both aligned and misaligned utility classes displayed similar trends.

C.3 Extended Results and Additional Modalities

We begin by introducing two additional utility families below:

Discounted cumulative gain (DCG).

We introduce the following discounted cumulative gain utility class, inspired by graded relevance evaluation (Järvelin and Kekäläinen, 2002). We note that this class highly resembles rank-based and topK\mathrm{topK} utilities in Example 3.6. Let γ∈ℝ+\gamma\in\mathbb{R}_{+} and define the discount sequence θr(γ)=(log2⁡(1+r))−γ\theta^{(\gamma)}_{r}=(\log_{2}(1+r))^{-\gamma} for ranks r∈[C]r\in[C]. For a prediction p=f⁡(X)p=f(X) and outcome Y=ejY=e_{j}, the realized gain is uγ​(p,ej)=θrank⁡(p,j)(γ)u_{\gamma}(p,e_{j})=\theta^{(\gamma)}_{\mathrm{rank}(p,j)} with associated regressor vuγ​(X)=∑if​(X)i​θrank⁡(f⁡(X),i)(γ)v_{u_{\gamma}}(X)=\sum_{i}f(X)_{i}\,\theta^{(\gamma)}_{\mathrm{rank}(f(X),i)}. Finally, for simplicity of evaluation, we used a fixed grid for γ\gamma and thus define the class 𝒰dcg≔{uγ∣γ∈{0.5,0.75,1,1.25,1.5,2}}{\cal U}_{\mathrm{dcg}}\coloneqq\{u_{\gamma}\mid\gamma\in\left\{0.5,0.75,1,1.25,1.5,2\right\}\}.

Semantic similarity utilities.

For ImageNet, we construct class embeddings E∈ℝC×dE\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times d} using the pre-trained Google News Word2Vec model (word2vec-google-news-300 loaded via gensim ) (Mikolov et al., 2013; Rehurek and Sojka, 2011). Class names are tokenized by lowercasing, replacing underscores/hyphens with spaces, and keeping alphanumeric tokens. For class ii, a class embedding EiE_{i} is the average of in-vocabulary token vectors. We compute the cosine similarity matrix S∈[−1,1]C×CS\in[-1,1]^{C\times C} such that Si,j=1S_{i,j}=1 if i=ji=j and Si,jS_{i,j} is the cosine similarity between EiE_{i} and EjE_{j}. Finally, we define the utility by expected similarity: uw2v​(p,ej)=∑ipi​S​[i,j]u_{\mathrm{w2v}}(p,e_{j})=\sum_{i}p_{i}\,S[i,j]. We denote this single-utility class by 𝒰w2v{\cal U}_{\mathrm{w2v}}.

The results are presented in tables and figures as follows. We note two general observations that illustrate the usefulness of our evaluation framework. (1) The order of performance among different post-hoc methods varies with respect to the evaluated utility class, stressing the need to account for downstream usage when evaluating calibration. (2) While post-hoc methods generally improve various metrics, eCDF plots reveal additional information. For instance, in multiple settings, post-hoc methods actively worsened (shifted to the right) the distribution of utility calibration errors.
